root.text.Letter to R Joseph son of Juda:
**IN THE NAME OF THE ETERNAL**
**GOD OF THE UNIVERSE**[^1]

[^1]: We have here translated the words אל עולם in the sense which Maimonides himself attributes to them in several places, and notably in chap. 29 of the third part of the *Guide*, although in the biblical passage (Genesis, 21, 33) these words signify *the eternal God*.

When[^1], my dear disciple Rabbi Joseph[^2], son of R. Iehouda [may he rest in paradise!],

[^1]: The verb كنت which begins the sentence relates to the words עטׄם שאנך, which it serves to put into the pluperfect.
[^2]: See my aforementioned Notice on Joseph ben Iehouda. We shall return to this disciple of Maimonides in the general introduction to this work.—The letters ש״צ, which follow the name of Joseph, are the abbreviation of שְׁמָרָהוּ צוּרוֹ, the Hebrew preterite being employed, after the Arabic manner, in the sense of the optative.

But when God decreed our separation, and thou didst depart in another direction, these conferences caused to be reborn within me a former resolution which had already become weakened, and thine absence impelled me to compose this treatise which I have fashioned for thee and for those like unto thee, however few in number they may be. I have formed it of detached chapters, and all that shall have been committed to writing shall reach thee successively wheresoever thou mayest be. Fare thee well.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.0: Cause me to know the way that I shall follow, for it is unto thee that I have lifted up my soul (Psalms 143, v. 8).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.1: It is you, O men, whom I call, and my voice (is addressed) to the sons of Adam (Prov. 8, 4).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.2: Give ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my science (Prov. 22, 17).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.4:
for the purpose of this entire treatise and of all that is of the same kind[^2] is the science of the Law in its reality; or rather, it has for its purpose to awaken the religious man in whose soul the truth of our Law is established and has become an object of belief, who is perfect in his religion and in his morals, who has studied the sciences of the philosophers and knows their diverse subjects, and whom human reason has attracted and guided to make him enter upon its domain, but who is embarrassed by the external (literal) sense of the Law and by that which he has always understood, or which he has been made to understand, of the meaning of these homonymous, or metaphorical, or amphibological names, so that he remains in agitation and in perplexity. Shall he let himself be guided by his reason and reject that which he has learned concerning these names? He would then believe himself to have rejected the foundations of the Law. Or shall he hold to that which he has understood of them,[^1] without letting himself be drawn away by his reason? He would thus have turned his back upon reason and would have removed himself from it, believing nevertheless that he had suffered a detriment and a loss in his religion, and persisting in those imaginary opinions by which he will feel himself disquieted and oppressed, so that he will not cease to experience sufferings in his heart and a violent trouble.

[^2]: The author intends to speak of the other works which he had himself composed upon this matter, such as certain parts of his commentary on the *Mishnah* and the first treatises of his *Mishneh Torah* or Abridgment of the Talmud.
[^1]: That is to say, that which he has understood in a superficial manner, by holding solely to the literal sense, which will lead him to corporealize the divinity and to admit other absurdities.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.5: This treatise has yet a second object: it is that of explaining very obscure allegories which are encountered in the books of the prophets, without it being clearly evident that they are allegories, and which, on the contrary, the ignorant and the heedless take in their exterior sense, without perceiving therein an esoteric meaning. Nevertheless, if a truly learned man examines them, there likewise results for him a violent agitation when he takes them in their exterior sense; but when we shall have explained to him (the meaning of) the allegory, or when we shall have apprised him that it is an allegory, he will be set upon the path and delivered from this agitation. It is therefore for this reason that I have called this treatise *Dalâlat al-'Hâyirîn* (the guide of those who are undecided or perplexed).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.6:
I do not say that this treatise will remove, for him who shall have understood it, every species of doubt; but I say that it will remove the majority of obscurities, and the most grave. The attentive man will neither demand of me nor hope, when we shall have spoken of a certain subject, that we should complete it, or, when we shall have commenced the explanation of the sense of a certain allegory, that we should exhaust all that has been said regarding that allegory: this, an intelligent man could not do by word of mouth, in a conversation[^1], and how could he commit it to a book without exposing himself to being a mark for every ignorant person pretending to science, and who would launch toward him the arrows of his ignorance.

[^1]: Literally: *for him with whom he would converse*.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.8:
Concerning matters of physics, it must be understood that there exist therein principles which also cannot be taught with clarity[^1] such as they are in reality. You are aware of that which the doctors say[^2]: "Neither (shall one interpret) the *Ma'asé beréschîth* before two persons"; now, if one were to explain all these things in a book, he would be *interpreting* them to thousands of persons. For this reason, these subjects also present themselves in the prophetic books by means of allegories, and the doctors likewise have spoken of them through enigmas and allegories, following the path of the (sacred) books, because these are matters which possess an intimate relation with metaphysical science, and which equally constitute a part of the mysteries of metaphysics.

[^1]: Instead of אלתצריח, one of the Leiden manuscripts bears: תצריחהא כל אלתצריח, a reading which Ibn Tibbon appears to have rendered by לגלותם · · · · · בביאור.
[^2]: See Mischnâ and Babylonian Talmud, *loco citato* [Lat.: in the place cited].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.10:
There are some among us for whom the lightning flashes time after time[^1], so that, as it were, they are constantly and without intermission surrounded by light, and the night becomes for them as the day; and this is the degree of the greatest of the prophets, to whom it was said: *And thou, stay here with me* (Deuteronomy, 5, 28), and of whom it was said: *For the skin of his face shone*, *etc*. (Exodus, 34, 29)[^2]. There are others for whom (the lightning) flashes but a single time in all their night, and this is the degree of those of whom it was said: *And they prophesied and did not continue* (Numbers, 11, 25). For others, finally, there are between each flash intervals more or less long.

[^1]: Ibn-Tibbon adds here, in his Hebrew version, the explanatory words במעט הפרש ביניהם *with small intervals*.
[^2]: The Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon adds here the following passage: ויש מי שיהיה לו בין ברק וברק הפרש רב והיא מדרגת רוב הנביאים. This passage is found in none of the Arabic manuscripts; it is likewise not found in the Hebrew version of Al-’Harizi, nor in the extracts of R. Schem-Tob ibn-Falaquera. See his *Moré ha-Moré*, printed at Presburg (1837, in-8vo), p. 9. Nevertheless, this passage also exists in the manuscripts of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, and it is reproduced by the commentators of that version, as well as by Samuel Zarza in his *Mekor ’hayyîm* or commentary on the Pentateuch at the book of Numbers, ch. 11, v. 25. This passage, moreover, is superfluous; for that which follows the words ויתנבאו ולא יספו says nearly the same thing.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.11:
But there are also those who do not attain to a degree (sufficiently elevated) for their darkness to be illumined by a lightning-flash; (it is so,) on the contrary, only as if by a polished body or some other similar thing, such as precious stones, etc., which shine in the darkness of the night. And even this small measure of light which shines for us[^1] is not continual; but it appears and hides itself as if it were *the glitter of the sword which turned* (Genesis, 3, 24).

[^1]: All the Arabic manuscripts bear עלינא. The word עליו in the editions of the version of Ibn Tibbon is an error; one must read עלינו, as indeed the manuscripts of this version have it.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.12: It is, then, according to these circumstances that the degrees of perfect men vary. As for those who never behold the light, but who wander in the night, those of whom it has been said: *They know nothing and understand nothing, they walk in darkness* (Ps. 82, 5); those from whom the truth is entirely hidden, however distinctly it may appear, even as it has been said of them: *And now they see not the light which shines in the heavens* (Job, 37, 21), and such is the generality of men; (as for those, I say,) there is no occasion to mention them here in this treatise.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.13: It must be known that, when one of the perfect men desires, according to the degree of his perfection, to express himself, whether verbally or in writing, upon something which he has understood in the matter of these mysteries, it is not possible for him to set forth even that which he has apprehended thereof with perfect clarity and in order, as he would do for the other sciences whose instruction is widespread. On the contrary, there will happen to him, in the instruction of others, that which happened to him in his own studies; I mean to say that the thing will appear and allow itself to be glimpsed, and that afterwards it will withdraw itself; for one would say that such is the nature of this thing, whether it be a matter of much or of little.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.16:
We had promised in the commentary on the Mischnâ[^2] to explain certain difficult subjects in (two works entitled): the *Book of Prophecy* and the *Book of Harmony*; the latter was a book in which we had promised to explain the obscurities of all the *Deraschôth*[^1], whose external words are in great disagreement with the truth and depart from the reasonable, and which are all allegories. But when, a number of years ago, we had commenced these books and had drafted a portion of them, the explanations into which we had engaged ourselves, according to this method, did not please us; for it seemed to us that by proceeding ourselves by way of allegory and by hiding what must remain hidden, we would not have departed from the primitive goal (of the *Deraschôth*), and we would have done nothing, so to speak, but substitute one individual for another individual of the same species; but that by explaining what has need of explanation, that would not suit the commonality of men, and yet we desired nothing else but to explain to the vulgar the sense of the *Deraschôth* and the external words of the prophecies. It seemed to us also that an ignorant man from the vulgar of the rabbis, in studying these *Deraschôth*, would find no difficulty therein: for he who is ignorant, indolent, and devoid of knowledge relatively to the nature of Being, does not find even impossible things to be improbable; whereas if, on the contrary, it were a perfect and distinguished man who studied them, one of two things would necessarily happen: either he would take them in the external sense, and then he would have a bad opinion of the author and take him for an ignorant man, but there would be in that nothing that could overturn the bases of the faith; or else he would lend them an esoteric sense, and then he would extricate himself well and would have a good opinion of the author, no matter whether the (true) interior sense of the words were clear to him or whether it were not. As concerns, moreover, the significance of Prophecy, the exposition of its diverse degrees, and the interpretation of the allegories of its books, all that will be explained in another manner in the present treatise. For all these motives, therefore, we have renounced composing these two works such as they had been (conceived); and we have confined ourselves,—in order to speak of the bases of the Faith and of general truths with brevity and by providing glimpses (of things) in a manner that approaches clear exposition—, to what we have said of them in the great talmudic work *Mischné Torâ*.

[^2]: See the introduction to the Xth (XIth) chapter of the treatise *Synhedrin*, at the seventh article of faith; *Porta Mosis*, by Pococke, p. 170.
[^1]: That is to say, the allegorical interpretations and the legends contained in the *Midraschîm* and in the *Haggadôth* of the Talmud.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.17:
As for the present treatise, I address my discourse therein, as I have said, to him who has studied philosophy and who has acquired the true sciences, but who, believing in religious matters, is troubled concerning their meaning, in respect of which obscure names and allegories[^1] leave some uncertainty. We shall also give in this treatise chapters in which there will be no question of any homonymous word. But such a chapter will serve as a preparation for another, or will call attention to one of the meanings of a homonymous word of which I should not wish to speak expressly in that place; such another chapter will explain some allegory, or will give warning that such a subject is an allegory; yet another will contain difficult subjects, in respect of which one sometimes believes the contrary of what is true, whether by reason of certain homonymies, or because one confounds the image with the thing it is intended to represent, or takes the thing represented for an image[^2].

[^1]: All the MSS. bear אלאםמא אלמשכלהֹׄ ואלאמתׄאל; instead of והמושאלים, which is read in most of the editions of the version of Ibn Tibbon, one must read והמשלים, as the MSS. and the *editio princeps* [Lat.: first edition] of 1480 bear it. It is singular that the same error should have crept into the unique MS. which remains to us of the version of Al-’Harizi, where one likewise reads והמושאלים. It would appear that it is the preceding word המםופקים which gave rise to the error, the copyists having believed that this word designated *amphibological* names; but the Arabic word אלמשכלה̈ designates, in general, the *obscure* names of the different categories mentioned at the commencement of this introduction.
[^2]: That is to say, in other words, that, on the one hand, one does not consider as an allegory that which is one, and that, on the other hand, one considers as an allegory that which ought to be taken in its literal sense. The commentary *Ephodi* cites as an example, on the one hand, the image of the adulterous woman (Proverbs, ch. VII), which, according to our author, designates matter, and which many commentators take in the literal sense, and, on the other hand, the narrative relating to Bathsheba (II Samuel, ch. XI, v. 2 et seq.), which evidently must be taken in its literal sense and in which certain commentators have seen an allegory.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.19:
The sage has said: *As apples of gold in networkings* (Maskiyyôth) *of silver, such is a word spoken according to its different faces* (Prov., 21, II)[^1].

[^1]: We translate this verse according to the explanation which the author himself is about to give of it.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.20:
Hearken to the explanation of the subject of which he speaks: *Maskiyyôth* are reticulated carvings, I mean where there are openings (formed) of extremely fine meshes, like the works of goldsmiths; they are so called because the gaze penetrates therein, for the Chaldaic version of וַיַּשְׁקֵף (he looked) is *we-istekhi*[^1]. He says, therefore: Like an apple of gold in a net of silver with very fine openings, such is the word spoken according to its two faces. And behold[^2] how this maxim applies marvelously to the regular allegory; for he says that the discourse which has two faces, that is to say, which has an exterior and an interior (meaning), must have the exterior beautiful as silver, but its interior must be yet more beautiful than its exterior, so that its interior shall be, in comparison with its exterior, as gold is beside silver. It is also necessary that there be in its exterior something which can indicate to him who examines it that which is in its interior, as it is with this apple of gold which has been covered with a net of silver with extremely fine meshes: for, if one sees it from afar or without examining it attentively, one believes it to be an apple of silver; but if the man of penetrating eye examines it right attentively, that which is within shows itself to him, and he recognizes that it is gold. And it is the same with the allegories of the prophets: their exterior words (contain) a wisdom useful for many things, and among others for the improvement of the state of human societies, as this appears in the exterior words of the Proverbs (of Solomon) and other similar discourses; but their interior (meaning) is a wisdom useful for beliefs having for their object the true in all its reality.

[^1]: The root of this Chaldaic word, according to the author, is the same as that of the Hebrew word *Maskiyyôth*.
[^2]: The form ארי (instead of ראוי or ראוי) is incorrect; nevertheless, as the author makes use of it very often and as it is found in all the manuscripts which we have consulted, we have thought it necessary to preserve it.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.21: Know also that prophetic allegories are constructed in two ways: there are some in which every word of the allegory requires (that one find therein) a (particular) meaning; and there are others in which the whole of the allegory reveals the whole of the subject represented, but wherein there are also words in great number which do not each add something to this represented subject, and which serve only for the embellishment of the allegory and for the symmetry of the discourse, or else to conceal with greater care the represented subject, so that the discourse is constantly conceived such as it ought to be according to the external sense of the allegory. This must be well understood.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.22: An example of the first species of prophetic allegories is found in this passage: *And behold, a ladder was set up on the earth, etc.* (Genesis, 28, 12); for the word *ladder* indicates a certain subject, the words *was set up on the earth* indicate a second, the words *and its head reached to heaven* indicate a third, the words *and behold, the angels of God* [tr. note: The French text reads *ct voici*, likely a typographical error for *et voici*.] indicate a fourth, the word *ascending* indicates a fifth, the words *and descending* indicate a sixth, and the words *and behold, the Eternal stood above it* indicate a seventh, so that every word which presents itself in this allegory adds something to the whole of the subject represented.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.23: An example of the second species of prophetic allegories is found in the following passage (Prov., 7, 6 and following): For through the window of my house, through my lattice I looked, and I saw among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths a child void of intelligence, who, passing through the public square near a corner, was advancing toward the house (wherein she dwelt). During the twilight, when the day was departing, in the obscurity of the night and in the darkness. And behold, a woman cometh to meet him in the attire of a courtesan and subtle of heart. She is clamorous, unsubdued, etc. Now in the street, now in the squares, etc. She seizeth him, etc. I owed peace-offerings, etc. Therefore am I come forth to meet thee, etc. I have covered with carpets, etc. I have perfumed my couch, etc. Come, let us intoxicate ourselves with love, etc. For the husband is not at home, etc. He hath taken the bag containing the money, etc. She seduceth him by the abundance of her speech, she draweth him away by her fallacious lips.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.25:
It is necessary to comprehend well that which I say, for it is a principle of great importance for that which I propose to explain. If, therefore, in a chapter of this treatise, you see me explain the sense of a certain allegory, and I direct your attention to the whole of the thing represented, you shall not demand of me [the explanation of] all the particular subjects which are encountered in that allegory, nor shall you seek to find the analogue thereof in the thing represented; for this would lead you to one of two things: either to cause you to lose sight of the subject which was intended in the allegory, or to impose upon you the task of interpreting [allegorically] words which are not subject to interpretation, and which were not written to be *interpreted*. And by imposing this task upon yourself, you would fall into that great folly with which the majority of the schools of the world are afflicted in our days, and which reveals itself in their writings[^1]; for each of these persons seeks to find a sense in words by which the author aimed at nothing of that which they themselves desire [to find therein]. You must, on the contrary, always have as your aim, in the majority of allegories, to know the whole of the matter which it was intended to make known; and in certain instances, it must suffice you to understand from my words that such a subject is an allegory, even though I should explain nothing further to you; for when you shall have known that it is an allegory, you will immediately understand what is its object, and by telling you that it is an allegory, I shall have, so to speak, removed that which was interposed [as an obstacle] between the sight and the object seen.

[^1]: Literally: *and in which they compose* [books].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.27:
I know that all beginners who have not yet pursued any speculative study will derive profit from certain chapters of this treatise; but perfect men, imbued with the study of the Law and who are troubled, as I have said, will profit from all its chapters, and how joyful they will be thereat, and with what pleasure they will listen to the reading thereof! But as for those confused persons whose brain is troubled by opinions contrary to the truth and by false methods, and who nevertheless believe these to be true sciences and claim to be men of speculative studies, while they know absolutely nothing that can in reality be called science,—as for those, (I say,) they will turn away from a great number of its chapters, and they will feel a great repugnance toward them, because they will not apprehend their meaning, and also because there will be recognized thereby the falsity of the base coin which they hold in their hands and which is their treasure and the fortune laid up for their distress[^1]. God the Most High knoweth that I have always felt a very great fear of committing to writing the things which I wish to deposit in this treatise; for they are hidden things, concerning which no book has ever been composed among our coreligionists in this time of captivity of which we still possess the works[^2]. And how then shall I be able to create something new and commit it to writing! Nevertheless, I have relied upon two principles: first, upon what (the Rabbis) have said concerning analogous things: *When it is the time to act for God, etc.*[^3]; secondly, upon what they have further said: *Let all thy works be done in the name of Heaven*. It is therefore upon these two principles that I have relied for what I have written in certain chapters of this treatise. Finally, I am the man who, seeing himself confined in a narrow arena and finding no means of teaching a well-demonstrated truth except in a manner which may suit a single distinguished man and displease ten thousand ignoramuses, prefers to speak for that one person, without paying heed to the blame of the great multitude, and claims to deliver that single distinguished man from the embarrassment into which he has fallen, and to show him the way (to go out) from his straying, in order that he may become perfect and obtain rest.

[^1]: The author means to say that they will flee from true doctrines because these will reveal to them all the falsity of the hypotheses and theories which they have imagined in order to silence their doubts and to appease the trouble of their soul, and which are, so to speak, their sole treasure, prepared in advance to save them from distress. It is here a question, doubtless, of those who followed the doctrines of the Motécalemîn. See above p. 5, note 1.
[^2]: The words אלתי ענדנא מא אלף פيهא, which are found in all the Arabic manuscripts, were omitted by the two Hebrew translators.
[^3]: It is known that the Rabbis lend to verse 126 of Psalms 119 the following sense: *When it is the time to act for God, it is even permitted to transgress the Law*, that is to say, one may allow oneself to violate some secondary precepts when it is a matter of consolidating the religious edifice in general.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.0:
PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION.

The causes of the contradiction or of the opposition which are found in a book or in any writing whatsoever are seven in number.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.1: FIRST CAUSE: When the author has assembled the sayings of persons of diverse opinions, while omitting (to cite) the authorities and to attribute each saying to its author. One then finds in his work contradictions or opposing assertions, because one of the two propositions is the opinion of one individual, and the other the opinion of another individual.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.2: S<small>ECOND CAUSE</small>: When the author of the book has first professed a certain opinion from which he has subsequently departed, and there have been collected both that which he had said at first and that which he said afterwards.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.3: T<small>HIRD CAUSE</small>: When the words (of the author) are not all (taken) in their exterior (literal) sense; but that some preserve their literal sense and others are an image and have a figurative sense, or else that the two propositions, contradictory according to their literal sense, are allegories, and that, taken in their literal sense, they appear contradictory or opposed to one another.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.4:
F<small>OURTH CAUSE</small>: When there exists a certain condition[^1] which, for whatever motive, is not expressly indicated in the passage itself, or else when the two subjects are different[^2] and neither of the two is clearly designated in the passage itself, so that there appears to be a contradiction in the discourse without there being one in reality.

[^1]: That is to say, when the two statements, or one of the two, must not be understood in an absolute manner, but under a certain reservation or implied condition. Thus, for example, when it is said, on the one hand, that God punishes the sins of the fathers upon the children (Exodus, 20, 5; XXXIV, 7), and on the other hand, that the fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children for the fathers (Deuteronomy, 24, 16), the rabbis, perceiving a contradiction in these passages, say that the punishment of the children for the sins of the fathers takes place *under the condition* that the children persist in the evil way of the fathers. — To cite another example, when one reads, on the one hand, that Moses entered *into the midst of the cloud* (Exodus, 24, 18), and on the other hand, that Moses could not enter into the tent of meeting *when the cloud rested upon it* (*Ib*., XL, 35), the rabbis say that he could enter into the cloud under the condition that he were expressly called there by the divinity.
[^2]: According to some commentators, the author means to speak here of two propositions containing homonymous subjects, and where, by taking the homonyms in the same sense, one might find an apparent contradiction. But the words of the author appear to have a more general sense. If, for example, it is said, on the one hand, that God reveals himself to certain prophets in a dream (Numbers, 12, 6), and, on the other hand, that dreams speak only falsehoods (Zechariah, 10, 2), the doctors, in order to make the contradiction disappear, say that it concerns dreams of a different nature, the ones true, the others false. See Babylonian Talmud, treatise *Berakhôth*, fol. 55 *verso*, Albo, ’*Ikkarîm*, l. III, ch. 10.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.5:
F<small>IFTH CAUSE</small>: The necessity (to which one is sometimes reduced) for teaching and for making (a certain thing) understood; that is to say, when there is a certain subject, obscure and difficult to conceive, which one needs to mention or to take as a premise, in order to explain a subject easy to conceive and which in teaching ought to precede that first subject, because one always commences with the easiest[^1]. It is then necessary that he who teaches should allow himself some latitude in order to make that first subject understood, in whatever manner it may be, by examining it in the gross without undertaking to set forth exactly its entire reality, and leaving it, on the contrary, within the reach of the imagination of the listener, so that the latter may understand what one wishes him to understand at that moment, reserving for later the more exact exposition of that obscure subject, which will be manifested in its reality in the proper place[^2].

[^1]: Moses of Narbonne, in his commentary, cites as an example the notions of *species* and of *genus* of which Aristotle had need to say a few words, when wishing to explain the category of substance (*Categories*, ch. III), although the exact explanation of these notions only comes later (in the *Topics*). The double nature, logical and ontological, of the categories and of various other notions of which the *Organon* treats, often necessitates the provisional and summary explanation of certain notions which are only truly fathomed in the metaphysics.
[^2]: The author says further on that, in his work itself, one finds certain contradictions resulting from the fifth cause. Let us cite an example of this: in chapter LXX of the 1st part, the author presents God as the immediate mover of the superior sphere, whereas at the end of chapter IV of the 2nd part he says that the first among the *intelligences of the spheres*, produced by God, sets in motion the first sphere. This is because, in the first passage, the author has no other aim than to present God as the *mover* of the universe in general, without entering into the details of the motion of the different spheres and of their *intelligences*, as he does in the second passage. There results from this a contradiction which is only apparent.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.6: S<small>IXTH CAUSE</small>: When the contradiction eludes notice and manifests itself only after several premises. The more premises are required to manifest it, the more it will be hidden, so as to escape the author, who will believe that there is no contradiction between the first two propositions. Nevertheless, by taking each of the two propositions separately and joining to it a true premise, so that a necessary conclusion results therefrom, and by doing the same with each conclusion—I mean, by joining to it a true premise so as to derive therefrom a necessary conclusion—one will arrive, after a series of syllogisms, at finding a contradiction or an opposition between the two final conclusions. This is what occurs even to learned authors; but if the first two propositions were manifestly contradictory and the author had merely forgotten the first while writing the other in another part of his work, that would be (to reveal) a very great inferiority, and such a man could not be counted among those whose words merit attention.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.8:
As for the contradictions which are found in the *Mischnâ* and in the *Baraïthôth*, they emanate from the first cause. Thus you will continually find it said (in the Talmud): “The beginning (of the chapter) is in contradiction with the end,” and that this response is added: “The beginning emanates from such a doctor and the end from such another doctor.” You will likewise find there these words: “Rabbi[^1] approved the words of such a doctor in such a case and simply reproduced his opinion (without naming him), and in such another case he approved the words of such another doctor and simply reproduced his opinion.” Often also you will find there this formula: “To whom belongs this anonymous assertion? It belongs to such a doctor. — To whom belongs our (paragraph of the) *Mischnâ*? It belongs to such a doctor.” These examples are innumerable.

[^1]: That is to say, Rabbi Judah the Holy, editor of the *Mishnâ*.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.9:
As for the contradictions and the divergences which are found in the Talmud (or the *Guemarâ*), they emanate from the first and the second cause. Thus you will always find therein these words: "Upon such a subject he adopted the opinion of such a doctor, and upon such another subject the opinion of such another doctor." It is further said: "He adopted the opinion of such a one in one case, and he departed therefrom in another case." Finally, it is said: "These are two *Amoraîm*[^1] (who differ) concerning the opinion of such a doctor." All examples of this kind are in conformity with the first cause. Relatively to the second cause, they (the Talmudists) say expressly: *Râb retracted such an opinion*, or *Rabâ retracted such an opinion*[^2], and (in such a case) it is discussed in order to know which of the two opinions is the last. One may further cite the following words: "According to the first redaction of Rabbi Asché[^3] he pronounced in such a sense, and according to the second redaction he pronounced in such another sense."

[^1]: It is known that the word אמוראי designates the doctors who figure in the *Guemarâ*, and who discuss the opinions of the *Tannaîm* or doctors of the *Mischnâ*.
[^2]: The manuscripts of the Arabic original generally contain both examples; the Hebrew version has only that of *Rabâ*.
[^3]: It is known that Rabbi Asché is one of the principal redactors of the Babylonian Talmud.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.10:
As regards the contradiction or opposition which appears in the external sense of certain passages of all the prophetic books, it emanates from the third and the fourth cause, and it is above all this subject which was the goal of this entire preliminary observation. You know that (the doctors) often repeat these words: "One text expresses itself in such a manner and another text in such another manner." They first establish the apparent contradiction, then they explain that there is therein a condition which is missing (in the text), or that it is a question of two different subjects. Thus, for example, they say: "Solomon, is it not enough that thy words contradict those of thy father? must they also contradict themselves, etc.?[^1]" The doctors often speak in this sense; but most of the time they occupy themselves with prophetic discourses relating to (religious) precepts or to morality. As for us, we had no other goal than to call attention to verses which, taken in their literal sense, contain contradictions on the subject of certain opinions and beliefs; a part of these will be explained in various chapters of this treatise; for this subject also forms part of the *Mysteries of the Law*. As for the question of knowing whether there exist in the books of the prophets contradictions emanating from the seventh cause, that is a matter which there is reason to examine and to discuss, and which must not be decided at random[^2].

[^1]: See Babylonian Talmud, treatise *Schabbâth*, fol. 30. Various passages are cited therein where Solomon is in contradiction with David or with himself, and one seeks to resolve the difficulty by establishing that in the contradictory passages different subjects are concerned. Thus, e.g., one reads in Proverbs (ch. XXVI, v. 4): *Answer not a fool according to his folly*, and immediately after (v. 5): *Answer a fool according to his folly*. To remove the contradiction, the Talmud says that, in one of the two passages religious things are concerned, and, in the other, profane things.
[^2]: Literally: *And one must not conjecture thereupon*. Ibn-Tibbon rendered the words אן לא יגׄזף פי דׄלך by a long periphrasis; Al-’Harizi translates more faithfully: וצריך לבל יגזרו עליו כפי מה שיזדמן.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.11: As for the divergence which is found in the books of the true philosophers, it emanates from the fifth cause.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.12: As regards the contradictions found in most of the works of authors and commentators other than those of whom we have spoken, they emanate from the sixth cause. Likewise, in the *Midraschôth* and in the *Haggadôth* there exist grave contradictions emanating from this same cause; wherefore (the Rabbis) say: "One does not raise objections regarding contradictions in the *Haggadôth*." One also finds therein contradictions emanating from the seventh cause.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.13:
Finally, the divergences which may exist in the present treatise emanate from the fifth and the seventh cause[^1]. It is necessary that thou shouldst know this, that thou shouldst imbue thyself therewith, and that thou shouldst well remember it, so as not to be troubled concerning several of these chapters.

[^1]: See above, page 28, note 1, and page 29, note 1.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.14: After these preliminaries, I begin to treat of the names of which it is necessary to elucidate the true sense intended in each instance according to the subject therein treated; and this shall serve as a key for entering into places whose doors are closed. And when these doors shall have been opened and one shall have entered into those places, the souls shall find rest therein, the eyes shall be delighted, and the bodies shall be relieved of their toil and their fatigue.
root.text.Part 1..0.0: OPEN THE GATES, THAT THE RIGHTEOUS NATION MAY ENTER, WHICH KEEPETH THE FAITH (Isaiah, xxvi, 2).
root.text.Part 1..0.1: *Célem* (צֶלֶם) and *demouth* (דְּמוּת). — There have been persons who believed that *célem* (צלם), in the Hebrew language, designated the figure of a thing and its lineaments, and this has led to pure corporification (of God), because it is said (in Scripture): *Let us make man in our image* (בצלמנו) *after our likeness* (Genesis, 1, 26). They believed, therefore, that God had the form of a man, that is to say, his figure and his lineaments, and there resulted for them that pure corporification which they admitted as a belief, thinking that, if they departed from this belief, they would deny the text (of Scripture), or even that they would deny the existence of God if He were not (for them) a body having a face and hands similar to their own in figure and in lineaments; only, they admitted that He was greater and more resplendent (than they), and that His matter also was not blood and flesh, and this is all that they could conceive of as most sublime with regard to God[^1]. [^1]: One would scarcely believe that Jewish doctors could have fallen into such errors, if we had not the positive testimony of Maimonides, as well as that of his son Abraham and of several of his contemporaries, who were obliged to undertake the defense of Maimonides against the attacks of several Talmudists, and notably against a portion of the rabbis of France, who believed they must take the anthropomorphisms of the Bible literally. We content ourselves with recalling in this regard the unsuspected testimony of a harsh adversary of Maimonides, R. Abraham ben-David of Posquières, in his critical notes on the *Mischné Torâ* or *Abridgment of the Talmud* (Book I, treatise *Teschoubâ* or of Penitence, ch. 3, § 7). Maimonides having counted among the number of heretics (מינים) him who admits the corporeity of God, R. Abraham asks: "Why does he call this one a *heretic*, since men greater and better than he (Maimonides) have followed this opinion, according to what they had seen in the texts of Scripture, and still more in the *Haggadôth* which trouble the thought?"
root.text.Part 1..0.2: As for that which must be said in order to remove corporeity and to establish the true unity—which has no reality save by the exclusion[^1] of corporeity—you shall know the demonstration of all this through the present treatise; here, in this chapter, one seeks only to call attention to the explanation of the meaning of *célem* (צלם) and of *demouth* (דמות). [^1]: Instead of בדפע (with *daleth*), several manuscripts bear ברפע (with *resch*), which changes nothing in the sense.
root.text.Part 1..0.3:
I say, then, that *form*, as it is generally known by the vulgar[^1] [I mean the figure of the thing and its lineaments], bears in the Hebrew language the particular name of *toar* (תאר); one says, for example: *Beautiful of figure* (תאר) *and beautiful of countenance* (Genesis, 39, 6); *what is his figure* (תארו) (I Sam., 28, 14)? *As the figure* (כתאר) *of the sons of the king* (Judges, 13, 18). It has been said (speaking) of *artificial form*: *He figures it* (יתארהו) *with the graver*... and *he figures it* (יתארהו) *with the circle* (Isaiah, 44, 13). This is a denomination which is never applied to God the Most High;—far from us (such a thought)!

[^1]: The author means to say that he does not employ here the word *form* in the philosophical sense, but in that of vulgar language.
root.text.Part 1..0.4: As for *célem* (צלם), it applies to the *natural form*, I mean to that which constitutes the substance of the thing, by which it becomes what it is and which forms its reality, insofar as it is such a (determinate) being. In man this something is that from which proceeds human *comprehension*, and it is by reason of this intellectual comprehension that it was said of him: *He created him in the image* (בצלם) *of God* (Genesis, 1, 26).
root.text.Part 1..0.5:
It is for this reason also that it has been said (speaking of the impious): *Thou shalt despise their image* (צלמם) (Ps. 73, 20); for the contempt reacheth the soul, which is the *specific form*[^1], and not the figures of the limbs and their lineaments. I say likewise that the reason for which the idols were called *celamîm* (צלמים), is that that which was sought in them was something which was supposed in them[^2]; but it was in no wise for their figure and their lineaments. I shall further say the same thing concerning the words: *the images* (צלמי) *of your* TE’HORÎM (I Sam., 6, 5)[^3]; for that which was sought therein was the means of averting the evil of the *te’horîm*, and it was in no wise the figure of the *te’horîm.* If, however, it were absolutely necessary to admit that the name of *célem*, applied to the images of the *te’horîm* and to the idols, referred to the figure and to the lineaments, this name would be either homonymous or amphibological[^4], and would apply not only to the *specific form*, but also to the *artificial form*, as well as to the analogous figures of physical bodies and to their lineaments.

[^1]: That is to say, the form particular to the human species, or that which characteriseth man and distinguisheth him from the other animals.
[^2]: Literally: *Their sense* (*their idea*) *which was imagined*, that is to say, the false idea which was formed of them, or the virtue which was attributed to them by error.
[^3]: It is generally believed that the malady of the Philistines, designated by the word *te’horîm* (טחרים) or, according to the reading of the *khetîb, ’apholîm* (עפלים), consisted in a species of tumours or of pustules in the secret parts; the rabbis see therein *haemorrhoidal varices*, and it is probably in this sense that Maimonides himself understandeth this word. The Jewish physicians of the Middle Ages commonly employ the word טחורים to designate *haemorrhoids.*
[^4]: See above, page 6, note 3.
