root.text.Part 1..1.0: A man of science put to me, already several years ago, a remarkable objection which merits consideration, as well as the response which we have made in order to destroy it.
root.text.Part 1..1.1: But before relating the objection and the manner of destroying it, here is what I have to say. Every Hebrew knows that the name *Élohîm* (אלהים) is homonymous, applying to God, to the angels, and to the governors ruling the states. Already Onkelos the proselyte has explained—and his explanation is true—that by the words: *And ye shall be as* Élohîm, *knowing good and evil* (Genesis, 3, 5), the last sense was intended; for he says (in his Chaldaic translation): “And ye shall be as *great personages* (כרברביא).”
root.text.Part 1..1.2: After this preliminary observation concerning the homonymy of this name, we shall relate the objection.
root.text.Part 1..1.5: Know that this word, I mean פקח, is employed absolutely only in the sense of: *opening the moral sight*, and is not used of the restoration of the sense of sight; for example: *And God opened her eyes* (Genesis, 21, 19); *Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened* (Isaiah, 35, 5); *Opening the ears, they hear not* (Ibid., 42, 20), which resembles these words: *They that have eyes to see and see not* (Ezekiel, 12, 2).
root.text.Part 1..1.6:
As for that which is said of Adam: *When he changed* face *thou didst send him away* (Job, 14, 20)[^1], it must be interpreted and commented upon thus: “When he changed *direction*, he was expelled”; for פנים (face, visage) is a noun derived from פנה (to turn), because man directs himself with his face toward the thing he wishes to attain. One says, therefore: When he had changed direction and had directed himself toward the thing toward which it had previously been forbidden him to direct himself, he was expelled from paradise. And this was a punishment equal to his disobedience, *measure for measure*[^2]; for it had been permitted him to eat of agreeable things and to delight himself in rest and tranquility; but having become greedy, having followed his pleasures and his imagination, as we have said, and having eaten that which it had been forbidden him to eat, he was deprived of all and forced to eat that which was most vile in the way of aliments, and that which had not served him as food before, (and this, moreover) by dint of pain and fatigue, as (Scripture) says: *Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee, etc., in the sweat of thy face, etc.* (Genesis, 3, 18, 19), and then it is clearly said: *And the Lord God sent him forth from paradise to till the ground* (Ibid., v. 23). And He assimilated him to the animals in his food and in most circumstances, as (Scripture) says: *And thou shalt eat the herb of the field* (Ibid., v. 18). And as if to explain this passage, (the Psalmist) said: *Man shall not abide in his dignity, and he was assimilated to the dumb beasts* (Ps. 49, 13).

[^1]: The author follows the opinion of the ancient rabbis who apply this verse to Adam: God, they say, had at first endowed Adam with an immortal strength (תתקפהu לנצח); but having neglected the counsel of God and followed that of the serpent, he was expelled from paradise. See *Beréschîth rabba*, sect. 14 and 21.
[^2]: That is to say, the punishment was entirely conformable to the sin; the Hebrew words מדה כנגד מדה, which the author here interpolates into the Arabic sentence, are a well-known proverbial locution, often employed by the rabbis.
root.text.Part 1..1.7: —Praise be to the Master of that will, the ultimate end and the wisdom of which cannot be comprehended.
root.text.Part 1..2.0: It is imagined that the meaning of *temounâ* (תמונה) and of *tabnîth* (תבנית) in the Hebrew language is the same; but it is not so. *Tabnîth* is a noun derived from בנה (to build) and signifies the *fabric* of a thing and its structure, I mean its figure, as for example the square, circular, triangular figure, etc. One says, for example: *The figure* (תבנית) *of the tabernacle and the figure* (תבנית) *of all its vessels* (Exod., 25, 9), and it is said again: *According to their figure* (כתבניתם) *which was shown to thee on the mountain* (*Ibid.*, v. 40); *The figure* (תבנית) *of any bird* (Deuteron., 4, 17); *The figure* (תבנית) *of a hand* (Ezek., 8, 3); *The figure* (תבנית) *of the porch* (I Chron., 28, 11). All this is a (*visible*) *figure*; wherefore the Hebrew language in no wise employs this species of expression in descriptions which relate to God.
root.text.Part 1..2.1:
As for *temounâ* (תמונה), it is a noun which is used by amphibology[^1] in three different senses. It is used, 1st, of the form of an object perceived by the senses independently of the mind, I mean of its figure and its lineaments; and such is the sense of the words: *..... and that ye shall make a graven image of the figure* (תמונת) *of anything, etc.* (Deuteronomy, 4, 25); *For ye saw no figure* (תמונה) (*Ibid.*, v. 15). It is used, 2ndly, of the imaginary figure which an object, after having withdrawn itself from the senses, leaves in the imagination, as in this passage: *In thoughts* (born) *of nocturnal visions, etc.* (Job, 4, 13 et seq.), which ends with these words: *It stood still, and I did not recognize its face; there was a figure* (תמונה) *before mine eyes*, that is to say, there was a phantom before mine eyes in sleep. It is used, finally, 3rdly, of the true idea (of a thing) perceived by the intellect, and it is in this third sense that one says *temounâ* in speaking of God; e.g.: *And he beholdeth the figure* (תמונת) *of the Eternal* (Numbers, 12, 8), which must be explained in this sense: *And he comprehendeth God in his reality*.

[^1]: See above, page 6, note 3.
root.text.Part 1..3.0: Know that the three verbs *raâ* (ראה), *hibbît* (הביט) and *’hazâ* (הזה) apply to the *sight* of the eye; but they are all three employed metaphorically for the perception of the intellect.
root.text.Part 1..3.1: As regards *raâ* (ראה), this is known to all. It is said, for example: *And he saw* (וירא), *and behold, there was a well in the field* (Genesis, 29, 2), where it concerns the *sight* of the eye; but in these words: *And my heart saw* (ראה) *much wisdom and science* (Ecclesiastes, 1, 16), it concerns an intellectual perception.
root.text.Part 1..3.2: It is in this metaphorical sense that the verb *raâ* (ראה) must be taken whenever it is applied to God, as for example in these passages: *I* SAW (ראיתי) *the Eternal* (I Kings, 22, 19); *And the Eternal made himself* SEEN (appeared) *to him* (Genesis, 18, 1); *And God* SAW *that it was good* (Genesis, 1, *passim*); *Make me* SEE *thy glory* (Exod., 33, 18); *And they* SAW *the God of Israel* (*Ibid.*, 24, 10). It is here everywhere a question of an intellectual perception, and by no means of the *sight* of the eye; for the eyes perceive only (that which is) body and (only) from a certain side[^1], and therewith some accidents of the body, such as its colours, its (geometrical) figure, etc., and God, for his part, does not perceive by means of an instrument, as shall be explained (further on). [^1]: The editions of the Hebrew version of Ibn Tibbon generally bear ובצדו קצת מקריו; one must read, according to the Arabic: ובצד וקצת מקריו, as indeed the manuscripts of the said version have it.
root.text.Part 1..3.3:
In like manner *hibbît* (הביט) is employed in the sense of: *to look* at a thing with the eye; for example: *Look not* (אל תבט) *behind thee* (Genesis, 19, 17); *And his wife looked* (ותבט), *being behind him* (Ibid., v. 26); *And he shall look* (ונבט) *toward the earth* (Isaiah, 5, 30). But it is employed metaphorically for the *regard* of the mind approaching the consideration of a thing in order to understand it, as in this passage: *One seeth not* (לא הביט) *iniquity in Jacob* (Numbers, 23, 21); for iniquity is not seen with the eye. It is the same with these words: *And they looked* (והביטו) *after Moses* (Exod., 33, 8); for, according to what the doctors say, they would express the same idea, and they would state that they (the Israelites) spied upon his acts and his words and examined them[^1]. The words: *Look* (הבט) *now toward heaven* (Genesis, 15, 5), have again the same sense; for that took place in a prophetic vision. And (in general) the verb הביט (to look) hath this metaphorical sense every time that it is applied to God; for example: ..... *to look* (מהביט) *toward God* (Exod., 3, 6); *And he beholdeth* (יביט) *the figure of God* (Numbers, 12, 8); *And thou canst not look* (והביט) *upon iniquity* (Habakkuk, 1, 13).

[^1]: That is to say, they criticized them and judged them with malevolence. The author alludes to various passages of the Talmud and of the *Midraschîm*. Thus, for example, the Jerusalem Talmud (*Biccourîm*, ch. III, and *Schekalîm*, ch. V) speaks of two doctors, one of whom had explained the passage in question in a sense of praise, and the other in a sense of blame; according to the latter, the Israelites said, in speaking of the stoutness of Moses: "See his thighs, see his legs; he eateth of that which belongeth to the Jews, he drinketh of that which belongeth to the Jews, all that he hath cometh from the Jews." ומאן דאמר לגנאי חזי שאקי חזי כרעין אכיל מן יהודאי שתי מן יהודאי כל מרליה מן יהודאי. See also *Midrasch Tan’houma*, sect. כי תשא (Verona edit., fol. 40 *d*); *Schemôth rabba*, sect. 51; Babylonian Talmud, *Kiddouschîn*, fol. 33 *b*. There were even some, saith the Talmud elsewhere, who went so far as to suspect him of adultery: שחשדוהו מאשת איש. See *Synhedrîn*, fol. 110 *a*.
root.text.Part 1..3.4: Likewise *’hazâ* (חזה) is applied to the sight of the eye; for example: *And let our eyes behold* (ותחז) *the fall of Zion* (Micah, 4, 11); and it is employed metaphorically for the perception of the heart, for example: ... *which he saw* (חזה) *concerning Judah and Jerusalem* (Isaiah, 1, 1); ... *the word of the Eternal to Abram* (במחזה) *in a vision* (Genesis, 15, 1); and according to this metaphor it was said: *And they saw* (ויחזו) *God* (Exod., 24, 11). Thou must well possess thyself of this.
root.text.Part 1..4.0:
The prince of philosophers,[^1] in entering upon the investigation and the demonstration of a certain most profound matter, expresses himself, by way of excuse, in terms the sense of which is: that the reader of his writings ought not, on the subject of his investigations, to tax him with impudence or (accuse him) of speaking temerariously and precipitately concerning things of which he knows nothing; but that he ought, on the contrary, to see therein only the passion and the zeal (with which he is animated) for producing and causing to be acquired true opinions, so far as this is within the power of man.

[^1]: One easily divines that the author intends to speak of Aristotle. In what follows, allusion is made to a passage of the *Treatise on the Heavens*, Book II, at the commencement of Chapter 12, where Aristotle, entering upon some questions relative to the motion of the spheres, expresses himself in nearly the terms which Maimonides here attributes to him.
root.text.Part 1..4.1:
We say likewise that man must not apply himself to this grave and important subject with precipitation, without having exercised himself in the sciences and branches of knowledge, and without having corrected his morals with the greatest care and killed his desires and his passions depending upon the imagination. It is only after having acquired the knowledge of true and certain axioms[^1], after having learned the rules of the syllogism and of demonstration, as well as the manner of preserving oneself from the errors of the mind, that he will be able to approach researches upon this subject. He must decide nothing according to a first opinion that might come to him, nor give free rein to his thoughts at the outset by directing them resolutely toward the knowledge of God; but he must employ therein modesty and reserve, and pause at times, in order to advance little by little.

[^1]: Literally: *after having obtained true and certain premises and having known them.* The word מקדמאת designates here the propositions which serve as premises in the syllogism; the author enumerates here all that forms part of the science of logic, which it is necessary to study deeply before approaching metaphysical subjects.
root.text.Part 1..4.2:
It is in this sense that it was said: *And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look upon God* (Exodus, 3, 6),—wherein one must also have regard[^1] to that which the literal sense indicates; namely, that he was afraid to look upon the resplendent light (of the burning bush),—not that the eyes could perceive the divinity [may it be exalted and elevated far above all imperfection!]. Moses merited praises for this, and the Most High poured out upon him His goodness and His favour to such an extent, that subsequently it could be said of him: *And he beholdeth the figure of God* (Numbers, 12, 8); for the doctors say that this was a reward for having at first *hidden his face so as not to look upon God*[^2].

[^1]: The author frequently employs the expression מצאפא אלי, *joined to, added to*, when he wishes to say that the literal sense may be admitted alongside the allegorical sense.
[^2]: In the Babylonian Talmud, treatise *Berakhôth*, fol. 7 *a*, it is said, among other things, in speaking of Moses: בשכר מהביט זכה לותמונת ה׳ יביט, "as a reward for having *abstained from looking*, he merited to *behold the figure of God.*" See also *Midrasch Tan’houma*, section שמות, edition of Verona, fol. 23 *b.*
root.text.Part 1..4.4:
If it was thus with regard to those persons, with all the more reason must inferior men such as ourselves and those who are below us aim first to occupy themselves with the perfection of their preparatory knowledge and to acquire preliminary principles which may purify the understanding of its defilement, which consists in errors; and then they will be able to advance[^1] to contemplate the holy divine majesty; for: *The priests also who approach the Eternal must sanctify themselves, lest the Eternal break forth upon them* (Exodus, 19, 22). Already Solomon has recommended the greatest precaution to the man who desires to attain to the degree in question; and, making use of an image, he has given this warning: *Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God* (Ecclesiastes, 4, 17).

[^1]: Instead of יתקדם some manuscripts have יתקדס (with *samekh*), *he shall be sanctified.*
root.text.Part 1..4.5:
I return now to complete that which I had begun to explain, and I say that, *the chosen among the sons of Israel* having made false steps in their perception, their actions also were thereby troubled, and they inclined toward corporeal things, by the vice of their perception; wherefore (the Scripture) saith: *And they saw God, and they did eat and drink* (Exodus, 24, 11)[^1]. As for the end of the verse (cited above)[^2], I mean the words: *And under his feet there was as it were a work of the brightness of sapphire, etc.*, it will be explained in several chapters of this treatise[^3].

[^1]: That is to say, after having seen God in their manner, they gave themselves up to corporeal enjoyments.
[^2]: The author intends to speak of verse 10: *And they saw the God of Israel*.
[^3]: See this 1st part, chap. XXVIII, and 3rd part, chap. IV.
root.text.Part 1..4.6: In sum, our purpose is to establish that whenever the verb ראה, or חזה, or הביט, is employed in the sense in question, it refers to an intellectual perception, and not to the *sight* of the eye; for the Most High is not a being whom the eyes can perceive.
root.text.Part 1..4.7: If, however, there be some limited man who does not wish to attain to that degree to which we desire to ascend, and who admits that all these words, employed in the sense in question, indicate the sensible perception of certain *created* lights, whether angels or something else, there is no harm in that.
root.text.Part 1..5.0: Isch (איש) and ischâ (אשה) are names employed primarily to (say) man and woman; subsequently they were borrowed to (designate) the male and the female of all other species of animals. It is said, for example: Of all clean quadrupeds thou shalt take seven couples, איש ואשתו, the man and his wife (Genesis, 7, 2); it is as if he had said the male and the female. Subsequently the name ischâ was employed metaphorically for every thing destined and ready to be joined to another thing; for example: The five curtains shall be joined אשה אל אחותה to one another (Exodus, 26, 3)[^1]. [^1]: Literally: the woman to her sister, the word יריעה being of the feminine gender.
root.text.Part 1..5.1:
It is clear therefrom that אחות (sister) and אח (brother) also, with regard to the figurative sense[^1], are employed as homonyms, similar to איש and אשה.

[^1]: The homonymy occurs in relation to the figurative sense, analogous to that indicated in the last instance for the word אשה.
root.text.Part 1..6.1:
It is in this same sense that he who has taught something to a person and has imparted to him an idea may be considered as having given birth to that person, he himself being the author of that idea; and it is in this sense also that the disciples of the prophets have been called בני הנביאים, *sons of the prophets*, as we shall explain when treating of the homonymy of the substantive בן, *son*[^1].

[^1]: It is evident that the author intended to devote a chapter, in this first part, to the word בן; but he did not do so.
root.text.Part 1..6.2:
It is according to this metaphor that it was said of Adam: *And Adam, having lived a hundred and thirty years, begat in his likeness, after his image* (Genesis, 5, 3); for it has already been stated previously[^1] what is signified by the *image* of Adam and *his likeness*. The reason is that all the children whom he had had previously did not possess (that which constitutes) the human form in reality, which is called the *image* of Adam and *his likeness*, and in respect of which it is said (that he was created) *in the image of God and in His likeness*. But as concerns *Seth*, (Adam) having instructed him and having given him the intellect, so that he attained to human perfection, it was said in his regard: *And he* (Adam) *begat in his likeness, after his image*. Thou knowest that whosoever has not obtained this *form*, the sense of which we have explained, is not a man, but an animal having the figure of man and his lineaments; but he possesses the faculty, which other animals do not possess, of doing every kind of harm and of producing evils. For the reflection and the thought which, in him, were destined to make him obtain a perfection which he has not obtained, he employs in every kind of artifice producing evils and in giving rise to harms; he is therefore, so to speak, something which resembles man or which counterfeits him. Such were the sons of Adam prior to *Seth*; wherefore it was said in the *Midrasch*[^2]: “Adam, during the hundred and thirty years that he was under reprobation, begat *spirits*,” that is to say, *demons*; but when he had obtained his grace, he begat his like, I mean *in his likeness, after his image*. This is what is expressed by these words: *And Adam, having lived a hundred and thirty years, begat in his likeness, after his image*.

[^1]: See above, chap. I, p. 37.
[^2]: See Babylonian Talmud, treatise *’Eroubîn*, fol. 18 *a*; cf. *Beréschîth rabba*, sect. 20 and 24, where the same thing is said in somewhat different terms.
root.text.Part 1..7.0: Makôm (מקום). — This name is primarily applied to the particular and common place[^1]; subsequently, language has extended its scope and made of it a name designating the degree and the rank of a person, I mean his perfection in any thing whatsoever, in such a manner that it is said: Such a one is in such a place (מקום), in such a thing (that is to say, having attained such a degree). You are aware of the frequent use made of it in our language when it is said: To fill the place (מקום) of one's fathers, for example: “He filled the place of his fathers in science or in piety,” and saying further: “The discussion remains in the same place,” that is to say, at the same degree. It is by this species of metaphor that it has been said: May the glory of the Eternal be praised in His place (Ezek., 3, 12), that is to say, according to the elevated rank which He occupies in the universe[^2]. And likewise, every time that use is made of the word מקום (place), in speaking of God, nothing else is intended but the rank of His existence, which has neither peer nor likeness, as shall be demonstrated. [^1]: That is to say, it applies at times to a particular place (ἴδιος) or to the place occupied by a particular body, at times to a common place (ϰοινός) more or less vast and containing several particular places (as, for example, the house containing dwellings, the city containing houses, the country containing cities, and so forth), and finally to the universal place or to space in general. Cf. Aristotle, Physics, bk. IV, ch. II. [^2]: Literally: according to His rank and His high dignity in Being. The words ועטׄם חטׄה are rendered in the version of Ibn Tibbon by ועוצם חלקו, and His great part; but Ibn Falaquera observes with reason that the word חטׄ has not here the sense of part, but that of כבוד, honor, dignity; for one could not say of God, the creator of the whole universe, that He has a part in that which is. See the appendix of the Moré ha-Moré, p. 149.
root.text.Part 1..7.1:
Know that whenever we explain to thee, in this treatise, the homonymy of a certain name, our purpose is not merely to awaken attention to that which we mention in the chapter itself, but we desire to open a door and to draw thy attention to the diverse meanings of the name in question, which are useful in relation to our purpose, and not in relation to the purpose of those who speak any vulgar language whatsoever[^1]. It is for thee to examine the prophetic books and the other books composed by the learned, to consider all the names employed therein, and to take each homonymous name in one of the senses which may be suitable to it in relation to the discourse (wherein it is found). That which we have just said is the key to this treatise and to others (of our writings).

[^1]: The author intends to say that, in the explanation of words, his purpose is solely to indicate the diverse philosophical meanings thereof, and that he does not concern himself with philological explanations, or with the various acceptations of words in the vulgar language.
root.text.Part 1..7.2: Thus, for example, (considering) the explanation which we have here given of the sense of *makôm* (מקום) in the passage: *May the glory of the Eternal be praised in His place*, thou shalt know that this same sense is that of *makôm* in the passage: *Behold, there is a place* (מקום) *by me* (Exodus, 33, 21), that is to say, a degree of speculation, of penetration by means of the intellect, and not of penetration by means of the eye, having regard at the same time to the *place* of the mountain to which allusion is made, and where the isolation (of Moses) took place in order to obtain perfection.
root.text.Part 1..8.0: *Kissé* (כסא) is employed primarily in the (Hebrew) language as the name for the *throne*; and, as the throne is occupied only by persons of distinction and grandeur, such as kings, and as, consequently, it is a visible thing[^1], indicating the grandeur of him who has been deemed worthy of it, his distinction and his high position, the sanctuary has been called *Kissé* (throne), because it indicates the grandeur of Him who manifested Himself there and who caused His light and His glory to descend therein. Thus (the prophet) has said: *A glorious throne, exalted from the beginning, etc.* (Jeremiah 17:12). It is again in the same sense that the heaven has been called *Kissé* (throne); for to him who knows it[^2] and who contemplates it, it indicates the grandeur of Him who caused it to exist, who sets it in motion, and who, by the good which He causes to emanate from it, governs the inferior world. We read, for example: *Thus saith the Lord, the heaven is my throne* (כסאי), *etc.* (Isaiah 66:1), that is to say, it indicates my existence, my grandeur, and my power, even as the throne indicates the grandeur of him who has been deemed worthy of it[^3]. [^1]: Literally: *an existing thing;* the word מוגוד appears here to have the sense of: *existing in a visible, sensible manner*. [^2]: That is to say, who has a scientific knowledge of it, who knows the spheres and their motions. [^3]: Some of the best manuscripts carry עלי עטׄים אהל לה, which does not offer a very satisfactory sense; Ibn Tibbon appears to have read עטׄים likewise, but this passage is somewhat corrupted in his version and offers variants in the different manuscripts and in the editions. Al-Harizi translates על גדולת מי שהוכן לו; one sees that he read עטׄם, but he has poorly rendered the word אהל. The reading we have adopted (עלי עטׄם מן) is that of three manuscripts; a fourth carries עלי עטׄמה̈ מן, which is the same thing.
root.text.Part 1..8.1: This is that which those who seek the truth must believe, and not that there is there a body upon which God is elevated; —how far is He exalted (above such a thought)!— For it shall be demonstrated to thee that the Most High is incorporeal, and how could He occupy a place or rest upon a body? But the matter is as we have remarked, namely, that every place which God has ennobled and distinguished by His light and His splendour, such as the sanctuary or the heaven, is called *Kissé* (throne).
root.text.Part 1..8.2:
If language has extended the use of this word by saying: *For the hand* (*is placed*) *upon the throne* (כם) *of God* (Exodus, 17, 16)[^1], this is again a qualification of His grandeur and His majesty, a thing which must not be represented as being outside of His essence, nor as one of His creatures, so that God would exist at one time without the throne and at another time with the throne. This would be, without doubt, an impious belief; for (the prophet) has clearly said: *Thou, Eternal, Thou residest eternally, Thy throne* (*remains*) *from generation to generation* (Lamentations, 5, 19), which indicates that (the throne) is a thing inseparable from Him. Thus, therefore, in this passage and in all other similar ones, one intends to designate by כםא (throne) the majesty and the grandeur of God, which are not at all something outside of His essence, as will be explained in several chapters of this treatise[^2].

[^1]: The author means to say: If a throne of God has been spoken of in passages where there is question neither of the sanctuary nor of heaven.
[^2]: See further on the chapters which treat of the attributes of God.
root.text.Part 1..9.0: We have already stated that whenever, in this treatise, we speak of one of the homonymous names, our purpose is not to mention all the significations in which this name is employed—for this is not a treatise upon language;—but we mention, of these diverse significations, those of which we have need for our purpose, and nothing else.
root.text.Part 1..9.1:
Among the number of these words (homonyms) are *yarad* (ירד) and *’alâ* (עלה); for these two words are employed in the Hebrew language in the sense of *descending* and of *ascending*. When a body transfers itself from one place toward another that is lower, one says ירד (to descend), and when it transfers itself from one place to another more elevated than that one[^1], one says עלה (to ascend). Subsequently, these two words were applied metaphorically to eminence and to greatness; so that, when the rank of a man has been lowered, one says ירד (he has descended), and when his rank has been raised in eminence, one says עלה (he has ascended). It is thus that the Most High has said: *The stranger that is in the midst of thee shall ascend* (יעלה) *higher and higher above thee, and thou shalt descend* (תרד) *lower and lower* (Deuteron., 28, 43). It is said again (employing derivatives of עלה): *And the Lord thy God will place thee above* (עליון) *all the nations of the earth* (Ibid., v. 1); and elsewhere: *And the Lord elevated Solomon very high* (למעלה) (I Chron., 29, 25). Thou knowest also that the doctors often employ this expression: “One must cause sacred things to *ascend*, but not cause them to *descend*”[^2].

[^1]: Instead of מן דׄלך אלמוצׄע some manuscripts bear מנה; likewise the two Hebrew versions ממנו.
[^2]: That is to say, it is permissible to give to sacred things a higher rank; but it is not permitted to make them descend lower. Thus, e.g., one reads in the Mischnâ (Part II, treatise *Schekalîm*, chap. VI, § 4) that as for the *shewbread*, they were placed first upon a table of marble and afterwards upon a table of gold; but it would not have been permitted to do the inverse. A community may sell lands in order to employ the price thereof to build a synagogue; likewise, with the money that has been received by selling copies of the *Prophets*, one may purchase copies of the *Pentateuch*; but it is forbidden to do the contrary (*Ibid.*, treatise *Méghillâ*, chap. III, § 1).
root.text.Part 1..9.2:
One expresses oneself still in the same manner (in speaking of thought): when the reflection of man lowers itself and his thought turns toward a thing most vile, it is said that *he has descended* (ירד), and likewise when his thought turns toward something elevated and sublime, it is said: *he has ascended* (עלה) [^1].

[^1]: As an example of this allegorical sense, the author cites, at the end of the chapter, the words: *And Moses ascended toward God*.
root.text.Part 1..9.4: Thus, therefore, whenever you shall find the expressions *to descend* and *to ascend* applied to the Creator, they can be understood only in the aforementioned signification.
root.text.Part 1..9.6: There has therefore (I say) been employed in this regard the expression *to descend*; for example: *Come, let us descend* (נרדה) *and there confound their language* (Genesis, 11, 7); *And God descended* (וירד) *to see* (*Ibid.*, v. 5); *I will descend* (ארדה) *and see* (*Ibid.*, 18, 21). The meaning of all this is the arrival of punishment upon the people here below.
root.text.Part 1..9.7: As for the preceding sense—I mean that of (divine) revelation and of ennoblement—it occurs frequently; for example: *I will descend* (וירדתי) *and I will speak with thee* (Numbers, 11, 17); *And the Lord descended* (וירד) *upon Mount Sinai* (Exodus, 19, 20); *The Lord will descend* (ירד) *before the eyes of all the people* (Ibid., V. 11); *And God ascended* (ויעל) *from over him* (Genesis, 35, 13); *And God ascended* (ויעל) *from over Abraham* (Ibid., 17, 22).
root.text.Part 1..9.8:
As for these words: *And Moses ascended* (עלה) *unto God* (Exodus, 19, 3), they possess the third meaning[^1], while stating at the same time that he *ascended to the summit of the mountain* upon which the created light[^2] descended; (but they signify) in no wise that God the Most High possesses a place to which one ascends or from which one descends. How far is He exalted above these imaginations of the ignorant!

[^1]: That is to say, the sense of an elevation of *thought*, which the author mentioned in the third place.
[^2]: That is to say, a light created expressly to represent the divine majesty (שכינה). See hereafter, chap. LXIV.
root.text.Part 1..10.0:
*Yaschab* (ישב). — The primary acceptation of this word in our language is that of *being seated;* e.g.: *And Eli the priest was seated* (ישב) *upon the seat* (I Sam., 1, 9). And, as the person seated is found established in the most perfect state of rest and stability, this word has been applied metaphorically to every stable and fixed state which does not change. It is thus that, in promising to Jerusalem at its highest degree (of prosperity) duration and stability, it was expressed: *And she shall be lifted up and seated* (וישבה) *in her place* (Zechariah, 14, 10). And elsewhere it is said: *He seateth* (מושיבי) *the barren woman in the house* (Ps. 113, 9), which signifieth: he establisheth her in a stable manner[^1].

[^1]: That is to say, God, by giving her children, assureth her a stable place in the house.
root.text.Part 1..10.1: It is in this latter sense that it has been said of God: *Thou, O Eternal, residest* (תשב) *eternally* (Lament., 5, 19); *Thou who residest* (היושבי) *in the heaven* (Ps. 123, 1); *He who residest* (יושב) *in the heaven* (Ps. 2, 4), that is to say, He who is perpetual and stable and who is subject to no species of change, neither change of essence, nor change with respect to any state whatsoever that might be outside of His essence, nor finally change with respect to His relation with another thing; for there is between Him and other things no such relation that He could undergo a change in that relation, as shall be explained hereafter[^1]. And by this it is perfectly established that He cannot change at all, in whatever manner it may be, as He has clearly said: *For I, the Eternal, I change not* (Malach., 3, 6), that is to say, by no change[^2]; and it is this idea which is expressed by the verb ישב (to be seated) when it is applied to God. [^1]: See hereafter, chap. LVI. [^2]: All the mss. bear תגירא; it is necessary to pronounce תַגִּירָא and to consider this word as an adverbial accusative.
root.text.Part 1..10.4: and it is further said: *The Lord sat* (ישב) *at the flood* (Ps. 29, 10), that is to say, when the things of the earth changed and perished, there was in God no change of relation, but that relation which he has with the thing[^1], whether the latter be born or perish, is a single, stable, and fixed relation; for it is a relation to the species of beings, and not to their individuals. Observe well that whenever you find the expression *to be seated* (ישב) applied to God, it will be in the sense in question. [^1]: The word אליה is put for אלי שי. Ibn Tibbon has paraphrased the word אליה by אל כל אחד מן הענינים ההם; Al-’Harizi has again here committed a misinterpretation by referring the suffix in אליה to God, and by translating this word as אליו לא לזולתו.
root.text.Part 1..11.0:
*Koum* (קום) is a homonym, and one of its significations[^1] is *to be standing*, as opposed to *to be sitting*; for example: *And he stood not up* (ולא קם) *nor moved for him* (Esther, 5, 9). It also contains the sense of *stability* and of *strengthening*, or *confirmation*; for example: *The Lord establish* (יקם) *his word* (I Sam., 1, 23); *And the field of Ephron was made sure* (ויקם) (Genesis, 23, 17); *The house that is in the walled city shall be established* (וקם) (Levit., 25, 30); *And the kingdom of Israel shall be established* (וקמה) *in thine hand* (I Sam., 24, 21). It is always in this sense that the word קום is said of God; for example: *Now will I arise* (אקום), *saith the Lord* (Ps. 12, 6; Isaiah, 33, 10), which is to say, now I will confirm my decree, my promise, and my threat; *Thou shalt arise* (תקום) *and have mercy upon Zion* (Ps. 102, 14), that is to say, thou shalt confirm the promise of commiseration that thou hast made to her.

[^1]: Some commentators ask why the author, in speaking of the proper and material sense of the verb קום, said: *one of its significations*, instead of saying: *its primitive signification*, or: *it signifies primitively*, as he ordinarily does in the explanation of homonyms. But they have not reflected that the primitive sense of the verb קום is *to rise*, whereas the explanations of the author relate to another signification of the same verb, that of *being standing*; it is this latter sense that he gives to the verb קום in the biblical passages he is about to cite. One will therefore no longer be astonished, with the commentator Shem-Tob, that the author, instead of citing passages from the Pentateuch, went to seek an example of the proper sense in the book of Esther; in the examples proposed by Shem-Tob, namely: ויקם אברהם (Genesis, 23, 3), ויקם פרעה (Exodus, 12, 30), the verb קום signifies *to rise*, whereas in the passage from Esther it may be translated as *to be standing*. Al-Harizi committed an error in translation by rendering וענינו לקום היושב ממקומו; by bringing out the sense of *to rise*, he did not realize the intention of the author, and he even altered his words. Ibn Tibbon translated literally ואחד מעניניו הקימה, taking קימה in the sense of the Arabic word קיאם, *to be standing*. Instead of מעניני, which the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version bear, one must read מעניניו, as it is found in the manuscripts.
root.text.Part 1..11.1: And, as he who is determined to do a thing is drawn toward the action by *standing upright*, it is said of anyone who feels himself incited to a thing that he *is standing*; e.g.: *For my son hath stirred up* (הקים, hath set upright) *my servant against me* (I Sam., 22, 8). This latter signification is also applied metaphorically to the execution of the decree of destruction pronounced by God against people who have merited punishment; e.g.: *And I will stand* (וקמתי) *against the house of Jeroboam* (Amos, 7, 9); *And he shall stand* (וקם) *against the house of the evil-doers* (Isaiah, 31, 2). It is possible that the words: "Now will I *stand*" (cited above) have this same sense; likewise these words: "Thou *shalt stand*, thou shalt have mercy upon Zion," that is to say, thou shalt rise up against her enemies.
root.text.Part 1..11.2:
It is this sense which is expressed in many passages, and there could be no question there[^1] of *standing* or of *sitting*, which would be unworthy of the divinity[^2]. "Above," say the doctors[^3], "there is no question either of *sitting* (ישיבה) or of *standing* (עמידה)"; for *’amad* (עמד) is employed in the sense of *kâm* (קם).

[^1]: By the word תׄם, *there*, the author means *with God*, in speaking of God.
[^2]: Literally: *May He* (God) *be exalted!* Instead of the elliptical expression תעאלי, one of the Leyden manuscripts bears תעאלי אללה ען דׄלך, *may God be exalted above that*, which appears to be a gloss, entered later into the text.
[^3]: See Babylonian Talmud, treatise *’Haghîgâ*, fol. 15 *a*; one sees that Maimonides admits in this passage the word עמידה, which the editors of the Talmud have erased to conform to the opinion of Raschi. Cf. Samuel Yaphé, *Yephé mareh*, at the beginning of the treatise *Berakhôth*.
root.text.Part 1..12.0: *’Amad* (עמד) is a homonym which has (firstly) the sense of *to be standing, to stand upright*; for example: *When he stood* (בעמדו) *before Pharaoh* (Genesis, 41, 46); *Though Moses and Samuel stood* (יעמד) *before me* (Jeremiah, 15, 1); *And he stood* (עמד) *by them* (Genesis, 18, 8). It has (secondly) the sense of *to abstain, to stop* (*to cease*); for example: *For they stopped* (עמדו) *and answered no more* (Job, 32, 16); *And she ceased* (ותעמד) *bearing* (Genesis, 29, 35). It has also the sense of *to be stable, to endure* (*to be preserved, to subsist*); for example: *That they may continue* (יעמדו) *many days* (Jeremiah, 32, 14); *Thou shalt be able to endure* (עמוד) (Exodus, 18, 23); *His taste remained* (עמד) *in him* (Jeremiah, 48, 11), it continued to subsist and to be preserved; *And his righteousness endureth* (עומדת) *for ever* (Ps. 111, 3), it is stable and permanent. Whenever the verb עמד is applied to God, it is in this latter sense; for example: *And his feet shall stand* (ועמדו), *in that day, upon the mount of Olives* (Zechariah, 14, 4), his causes, I mean the (events) caused by him, *shall subsist, shall be confirmed*. This will be further explained when we speak of the homonymy of the word רגל (foot)[^1]. It is in this sense also that one must take the words of God addressed to Moses[^2]: *But as for thee, stand thou* (עמד) *here by me* (Deuter., 5, 28), and (these words of Moses): *I stood* (אנכי עמד) *between the Lord and you* (*Ibid.*, v. 5)[^3]. [^1]: See hereafter, chap. XXVIII. [^2]: The words קולה לה תעאלי are for קולה תעאלי למשה. [^3]: The author does not clearly explain his thought; according to the commentators, Maimonides means that the verb עמד, in the two last passages, applies to the stable and permanent part of Moses, that is to say, to his intellectual soul, and to the union of the latter with the active intellect and with God.
root.text.Part 1..13.0:
As for the homonymy of the word *Adam* (אדם), it is first the name of the first man, a derivative name[^1], which, according to the text (of Scripture), comes from *adamâ* (אדמה, earth)[^2]; next, it is the name of the species; e.g.: *My spirit shall no longer plead with man* (באדם) (Genesis, 6, 3); *Who knoweth if the spirit of the sons of men* (בני האדם), *etc.* (Ecclesiastes, 3, 21); *The advantage of man* (האדם) *over the beast is nothing* (ibid., v. 19). It is also a name to (designate) the multitude, I mean the vulgar to the exclusion of distinguished persons; e.g.: *Both the vulgar men* (בני אדם) *and the distinguished men* (Psalms 49, 3).

[^1]: The first משתק is found in all the mss.; it was not rendered in the version of Ibn Tibbon.
[^2]: Maimonides, as well as other commentators, finds the indication of this etymology in Genesis, chap. 2, v. 7, and ch. III, v. 23.
root.text.Part 1..13.1:
In this third sense (it is found also in the following verses): *And the sons of the Élohîm*[^1] *saw the daughters of* MAN (Genesis, 6, 2); *Verily, ye shall die like vulgar* MAN (Ps. 82, 7).

[^1]: Concerning the different significations of the word *Élohîm* (אלהים), see ch. II, at the beginning.
root.text.Part 1..14.0: *Naçab* (נצב) or *yaçab* (יצב). — Although these two roots are different, they have, as you know, the same sense in all their forms of conjugation.
root.text.Part 1..14.1: It is a homonym which sometimes has the sense of *to stand upright, to arise*; e.g., *And his sister stood* (ותתצב) *afar off* (Exodus, 2, 4); *The kings of the earth set themselves* (יתיצבו) (Ps. II. 2); .... *came out, and stood* (נצבים) (Numbers, 16, 27); sometimes that of *being stable, permanent*; e.g., *Thy word standeth* (נצב) *in heaven* (Ps. 119, 89), that is to say, *stable* and *permanent*.
root.text.Part 1..14.2: Whenever this word is employed in relation to the Creator, it has this latter sense; e.g.: *And behold, the Eternal standing* (נצב) *above* (Genesis, 28, 13), being stable and permanent *above it*, that is to say, above the ladder of which one extremity is in heaven and the other upon the earth, and upon which all those who mount spring forth[^1] and ascend, in order to perceive Him who is above of necessity[^2]; for He is stable and permanent at the head of the ladder. [^1]: The word יתםלק, which is found in all the manuscripts, has not been rendered in the version of Ibn Tibbon. [^2]: The adverb צׄרורה̈ does not relate to ידרך, but to מן עליה; the sense is: *He* who is *necessarily* on high, the absolute and necessary Being.
root.text.Part 1..14.4:
I return to our subject, namely that (in the passage in question), נצב signifies *stable, perpetual, permanent*, and not *to be standing* like a body. In the same sense also (must this passage be explained): *And thou shalt stand* (ונצבת) *upon the rock* (Exodus, 33, 21)[^1]; for thou hast already understood that *naçab* (נצב) and *’amad* (עמד) have in this regard the same sense[^2], and indeed God said: *Behold, I will stand* (עומד) *there before thee upon the rock, in Horeb* (Ibid., 17, 6)[^3].

[^1]: The author sees in this passage an allusion to the perpetual contemplation of God by Moses. See the following chapter on the word צור.
[^2]: That is to say, that the two verbs are employed figuratively when they relate to something stable and imperishable.
[^3]: By this last example, the author wishes to show that the verb *’amad*, placed in relation with the substantive צור, *rock*, forms an allegory representing the permanence of the action of God in the universe and of His inspiration communicating itself to Moses; he infers from this that, in the verse cited previously, the word *naçab*, placed in relation with the same substantive, must form an analogous allegory. Here it is the spirit of God which penetrates Moses; there it is the intellect of Moses uniting with God through contemplation.
root.text.Part 1..0.8: Now, as man is distinguished by something most remarkable within him, which is found in none of the beings beneath the sphere of the moon—that is to say, by intellectual apprehension, for which neither sense, nor hands, nor arms are employed[[fn:67]], is used to designate [[t:0]]the hand;[[t:1]] [[t:2]]ׂגאנחה̈[[t:3]] is used to designate [[t:4]]the ribs[[t:5]], and appears also to be used for [[t:6]]ׂגנאח[[t:7]] [[t:8]]جناح[[t:9]] [[t:10]]wing[[t:11]], and, like the latter, in the sense of [[t:12]]arm.[[t:13]] The version of Ibn Tibbon reads: [[t:14]]ולא מעשה גוף ילא יד ולא רגל[[t:15]], which is not entirely exact; yet this translation is preferable to that of Al-Harizi, which reads: [[t:16]]לא אבר ולא נתח[[t:17]].[[t:18]], (this) has been compared to the divine apprehension, which is not effected by means of an instrument; although the resemblance does not exist in reality, but only at first sight. And for this reason, I mean because of the divine intellect which joins itself to man[[fn:68]], or the union of [[t:19]]the active intellect[[t:20]] (proceeding from God through the mediation of the Intelligences of the spheres) with [[t:21]]the passive intellect.[[t:22]] This subject will be explained in several places in this work. See hereafter ch. LXVIII; Part II[[t:23]]nd[[t:24]], ch. IV; Part III[[t:25]]rd[[t:26]], ch. LI, and other places.[[t:27]], it was said of him that he was (made) [[t:28]]in the image of God and in His likeness[[t:29]], (and this signifies) in no wise that God the Most High is a body having any figure whatsoever.
root.text.Part 1..1.3: It would appear, according to the literal sense of the text, said the author of the objection, that the primitive intention in (the creation of) man was that he should be as the rest of the animals, without intelligence and without reflection, and without the knowledge to distinguish between good and evil; but that, having disobeyed, his disobedience merited for him this great perfection peculiar to man, that is to say, the possession of that discernment which is within us, which is the noblest element of our existence and which constitutes our substance. Yet it is a marvelous thing that his punishment for his disobedience should have been the bestowal of a perfection which he had not previously possessed, namely, intelligence. This is altogether like the assertion of those who have said that a certain man, after having disobeyed (God) and committed excesses of injustice, was transformed and placed as a star in the heavens[[fn:69]], and who is said to have been placed in the heavens by identifying him with the constellation of the [[t:0]]Giant[[t:1]] [[t:2]](الجبّار)[[t:3]] or of [[t:4]]Orion.[[t:5]] See the [[t:6]]Chronicon Paschale [Lat.: Paschal Chronicle][[t:7]], p. 36; on the [[t:8]]Djebbâr[[t:9]] or [[t:10]]Orion[[t:11]] see the commentary on the treatise of Ulugh Beg, by Hyde, in the [[t:12]]Syntagma dissertationum [Lat.: Collection of Dissertations][[t:13]], volume I, pages 42 et seq., and p. 57.[[t:14]].—Such was the scope and the thought of the objection, although it was not (presented) in these very terms.
root.text.Letter to R Joseph son of Juda: thou didst present thyself before me, having come from a distant land[[fn:3]]. Joseph had come from Sabta or Ceuta, situated in the north-west of Africa, which the Arabs called [[t:0]]Al-Maghreb al-Akça[[t:1]] or the extreme West. See the aforementioned Notice, pages 6 and 14.[[t:2]] to follow my lessons, thou wert already very high in my esteem because of thy great passion for study, and because I had recognized in thy poems a very pronounced love for speculative matters, and this since thy opuscules and thy [[t:3]]Makâmât[[t:4]][[fn:4]] among the Arabs are short stories or narratives written in rhymed prose mingled with verse; the famous [[t:5]]Makâmât[[t:6]] or [[t:7]]Assemblies[[t:8]] of Harizi are well known. This genre of composition was imitated in Hebrew by the Jews from the first half of the XII[[t:9]]th[[t:10]] century, and they were given the name of [[t:11]]מחברות[[t:12]]; it is indeed this word that R. Yehuda al-Harizi employs here in his translation, and which renders the sense of the Arabic word much better than the word [[t:13]]חרוזיך[[t:14]], employed by Ibn Tibbon. Al-Harizi, in his collection of Makâmât known under the title of [[t:15]]Ta’hkemôni[[t:16]] ([[t:17]]תחכמוני[[t:18]]), himself cites from our Joseph a [[t:19]]Makâma[[t:20]] which had become famous. See my aforementioned Notice, p. 48 et seq.[[t:21]] had reached me from Alexandria, and before I could (by myself) test thy conception. I said to myself (at first): Perchance his desire is stronger than his understanding; but when thou hadst completed, under my direction, thy studies in astronomy and the mathematical sciences which thou hadst previously approached and which must necessarily serve as a preparation for it, I felt toward thee a much greater joy because of the excellence of thy mind and the quickness of thy conception; and, seeing that thou hadst a great love for mathematics, I left thee free to exercise thyself therein, knowing what thy future was to be[[fn:5]] of Hyde, published by Sharpe, vol. I, p. 436.) This reading is found in none of the Oxford manuscripts, nor in the two mss. of Leyden.[[t:22]]. And when thou hadst completed under me thy studies in logic, my hope was fixed upon thee and I judged thee worthy that I should reveal to thee the mysteries of the prophetic books, so that thou mightest understand therein what perfect men ought to understand. I began, therefore, to give thee glimpses of things and to provide thee with certain indications; but I saw thee asking more of me, and thou didst insist that I should explain to thee subjects belonging to metaphysics and that I should make known to thee in this regard what the [[t:23]]Mutakallimûn[[t:24]][[fn:6]] in several places of this work, and notably Part I[[t:25]]st[[t:26]], ch. 71, 73 et seq. I have given a succinct overview of their doctrines in the [[t:27]]Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques[[t:28]], art. [[t:29]]Arabes[[t:30]].[[t:31]] aimed at, and whether their methods were based upon demonstration, or, in the contrary case, to what art they belonged. I saw that thou hadst already somewhat studied this matter under other (masters); but thou wert agitated and seized with troubles[[fn:7]], so that the words [[t:32]]אלדהשה̈[[t:33]] [[t:34]]ברח[[t:35]] signify: [[t:36]]trouble[[t:37]] or [[t:38]]confusion had taken possession of thee[[t:39]]. Ibn Tibbon has well rendered the word [[t:40]]בלחך[[t:41]] by [[t:42]]דפקתך[[t:43]].[[t:44]], and thy noble soul stimulated thee [[t:45]]in order to find the objects of thy desire[[t:46]][[fn:8]]. I did not cease to turn thee away from this path and I recommended thee to take things in order; for my aim was (to ensure) that the truth should be established for thee methodically and that certainty should not come to thee as if by chance. So long as thou wert with me, I did not refuse, when there was question of a verse or of one of the texts of the doctors calling attention to some curious subject, to give thee the explanation thereof;
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.3: This treatise has for its primary object the explanation of the meaning of certain names[[fn:9]] the author here understands not only substantives and adjectives, but also verbs in the infinitive or [[t:0]]verbal nouns[[t:1]].[[t:2]] which occur in the prophetic books. Among these names there are some which are homonymous, but which the ignorant take in one of the senses in which the homonym is employed; others are metaphorical, and are taken in the primitive sense from which the metaphor is borrowed; others, finally, are amphibological, so that at times they are believed to be employed as appellative names[[fn:10]] or [[t:3]]appellative[[t:4]] is called by the Arabs [[t:5]]الاسم المتواطئ[[t:6]] , or else [[t:7]]الاسم المقول بتواطؤ[[t:8]] , that is to say, [[t:9]]conventional name[[t:10]] or [[t:11]]stated by convention[[t:12]]. The rabbis have translated these terms by [[t:13]]השם המוסכם[[t:14]] and [[t:15]]השם הנאמר בהסכמה[[t:16]]; the definition thereof may be seen in the [[t:17]]Compendium of Logic[[t:18]] ([[t:19]]באור מלות ההגיון[[t:20]]) of Maimonides, ch. 13. The Arabic term [[t:21]]بتواطؤ[[t:22]] corresponds to the Greek words [[t:23]]κατὰ συνθήκην[[t:24]], and is borrowed from the Arabic translation of the [[t:25]]Organon[[t:26]] of Aristotle; see the treatise [[t:27]]On Interpretation[[t:28]], at the beginning of ch. II, where the words: [[t:29]]Ὄνομα μὲν οὖν ὲστι φωνὴ σημαντικὴ κατὰ συνθὴκην[[t:30]] are thus rendered in Arabic: [[t:31]]فالاسم هو لفظة دالة بتواطؤ[[t:32]] (Ar. Ms. of the Bibl. nat., no. 882 A).[[t:33]] and at other times it is imagined that they are homonymous[[fn:11]], e.g., may be applied to the living man, as well as to the dead man, or to a statue, or to a portrait. If one has regard only to the external form, the word [[t:34]]man[[t:35]], taken in these various senses, may be considered as a true appellative, or common name, designating all that outwardly presents the human form; but if one has regard to that which constitutes the true essence of man, the word [[t:36]]man[[t:37]], taken in the various senses indicated, will be a homonym, since it designates at once things of diverse nature. From this point of view, the word [[t:38]]man[[t:39]] is called [[t:40]]اسم مشكك[[t:41]] , [[t:42]]ambiguous name[[t:43]] or [[t:44]]amphibological[[t:45]]. See Maimonides, [[t:46]][Lat.: loco citato][[t:47]], and the present work, Part I[[t:48]]st[[t:49]], ch. 56 (fol. 68 [[t:50]]b[[t:51]] of our Arabic text).[[t:52]]. The object of this treatise is by no means to make all these names understood by the commonality of men or by those who are beginning to study, nor to instruct him who studies only the science of the Law, I mean its traditional interpretation[[fn:12]];
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.7: We have already given in our Talmudic works[[fn:16]] several summary explanations of this kind and awakened attention to many subjects, and we have therein remarked that the [[t:0]]Ma'asé beréschîth[[t:1]] (account of the creation) is physical science and the [[t:2]]Ma'asé mercabâ[[t:3]] (account of the celestial chariot) is metaphysical science[[fn:17]], in the 1[[t:4]]st[[t:5]] chapter of Ezekiel and in some passages of Isaiah and Zechariah. The visions of these prophets, and notably those of Ezekiel, are designated by the name of [[t:6]]Ma’asé mercabâ[[t:7]], or [[t:8]]account of the chariot[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]celestial[[t:11]]). The mysteries of [[t:12]]Beréschîth[[t:13]] and of the [[t:14]]Mercabâ[[t:15]] play a great part in the writings of the Kabbalists, who are little in agreement as to what must be understood by these mysteries, the Talmud not having pronounced upon this matter. Maimonides, who was no partisan of the Kabbalah, speaks nevertheless, as a Talmudist, of the [[t:16]]Ma’asé beréschîth[[t:17]] and of the [[t:18]]Ma’asé mercabâ[[t:19]], and, imbued with the philosophical doctrines of the Arabian schools, he explains both in such a manner as to find therein the principal parts of the Peripatetic philosophy, seeing in the one the [[t:20]]physics[[t:21]] and in the other the [[t:22]]metaphysics[[t:23]] of Aristotle. It is in this sense that he already speaks of them in his Talmudic works. See [[t:24]]Commentary on the Mishnah[[t:25]], II[[t:26]]nd[[t:27]] part, treatise Hagigah, ch. II, § 1; [[t:28]]Abridgment of the Talmud[[t:29]], book I, 1[[t:30]]st[[t:31]] treatise (or [[t:32]]Yesodé ha-Torah[[t:33]]), ch. 1 to 4.[[t:34]], and we have explained this sentence[[fn:18]], even to a single pupil in particular, unless he be a subject of superior intelligence.[[t:35]]: “Neither (shall one interpret) the [[t:36]]mercabâ[[t:37]], even to one (pupil) alone, unless he be a wise man understanding by his own intelligence, (and in this case) one shall transmit to him only the first elements.” Thou shalt therefore ask of me here nothing other than the first elements. These very elements are not found, in the present treatise, arranged in order and in a continuous manner, but, on the contrary, disseminated and mingled with other subjects which one desired to explain; for my purpose is (to ensure) that the truths may be glimpsed therein, and that they may then withdraw, so as not to be in opposition to the divine purpose, which indeed it would be impossible to oppose, and which has caused the truths that have particularly for their object the understanding of God to be hidden from the commonality of men, as (the Psalmist) has said: [[t:38]]The secret of the Lord is with them that fear Him[[t:39]] (Ps. 25:14).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.9: It must not be believed that there is a single one among us who knows these grave mysteries in all their extent[[fn:21]].[[t:0]]. It is not so; but, on the contrary, the truth sometimes appears to us in such a way as to seem (clear as) the day, and sometimes it is hidden by material and common things[[fn:22]], that is to say, things pertaining to matter and to daily life. Ibn-Tibbon has rendered the word [[t:1]]אלמואדּ[[t:2]] (matters) by [[t:3]]הטבעים[[t:4]], and Al-Harizi by [[t:5]]כהות הטבע[[t:6]], which appears to me inexact.[[t:7]], so that we fall back into a profound night much as we were before, and we are then like the man who, finding himself in a profoundly dark night, sometimes sees a flash of lightning shine therein.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.14: Wherefore all learned metaphysicians and theologians[[fn:26]] or [[t:0]]Rabbanite[[t:1]], but that of [[t:2]]theologian[[t:3]] or [[t:4]]metaphysician[[t:5]], much like the word [[t:6]]אלאהי[[t:7]], which precedes it; it is derived from [[t:8]]رَبّ[[t:9]], in the sense of [[t:10]]master[[t:11]] par excellence, or of [[t:12]]God[[t:13]]. It is thus that Ibn-Tofail calls the intellectual faculty of man [[t:14]]امر ربانی الاهی[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]Epistola de Hai Ebn-Yokdhan [Lat.: Epistle of Hai Ebn-Yokdhan][[t:17]], ed. Pocock, p. 137). See also the observations of R. Shem-Tob Ibn-Falaquera on the version of Ibn-Tibbon, [[t:18]]Moré ha-Moré[[t:19]], p. 148.[[t:20]], friends of truth, when they wished to teach anything of this kind, spoke of it only by allegories and enigmas, and, multiplying allegories, they employed them of different species and even of different genera; they formed most of them in such a way as to make understood the subject one had in view, either at the beginning of the allegory, or in the middle, or at the end, unless an image could be found which applied to the thing in question from the beginning to the end. (Sometimes) also the subject which one aimed to teach the student, although it were a subject essentially [[t:21]]one[[t:22]], was divided, by placing it in several allegories remote from one another; but what is yet more obscure is when one and the same allegory is employed for diverse subjects, so that the beginning of the allegory applies to a certain subject and the end to another. Sometimes also the whole allegory is employed for two analogous subjects[[fn:27]] in this kind of science. Finally, when anyone wished to teach without the use of allegories and enigmas, there was in his words an obscurity and a brevity which took the place of the use of allegories and enigmas. One would say that the learned and the doctors are guided in this respect by the divine will, even as their physical dispositions guide them (in other respects).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.24: The whole of this discourse is intended to warn that one must not follow the pleasures and passions of the body; he therefore compares matter, which is the cause of all these bodily passions, to a courtesan who is at the same time a married woman, and it is upon this allegory that he has constructed his entire book. In several chapters of this treatise we shall show how wise it was on his part to compare matter to an unfaithful married woman, and we shall observe how he concluded his book with the praise of the woman who is not unfaithful, but who occupies herself only with the good order of her house and the position of her husband. (It will also be seen that) all the obstacles which prevent man from attaining his final perfection, every vice and every sin which attach to man, arise only from the side of matter alone, as we shall explain in this treatise. It is, then, this general doctrine which forms the content of this entire allegory; I mean that man must not follow his animal nature alone, that is to say, his matter; for the proximate matter of man is also the proximate matter of other animals[[fn:40]] or by [[t:0]]proximate[[t:1]] the author understands all that constitutes the animal organism, such as, for example, the members of the body, the flesh, the blood, the humours, etc.; for, in this respect, man perfectly resembles the animals, and forms with them one and the same species. The elements form a more [[t:2]]remote[[t:3]] and more general matter, embracing all sublunary bodies. The most remote and most general matter is the [[t:4]]prime matter[[t:5]] or the hyle [[t:6]]ג[[t:7]] which embraces the whole of creation.[[t:8]]. After having given thee this explanation and having revealed to thee the mystery of this allegory, thou wilt no longer hope[[fn:41]] to be able to ask me what there is (hidden) beneath the words: [[t:9]]I had peace offerings with me; this day have I paid my vows;[[t:10]] what meaning is contained in the words: [[t:11]]I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry[[t:12]]; or what is added to the general sense by the words: [[t:13]]For the goodman is not at home[[t:14]], as well as all that follows in this chapter. All this is but a series of phrases relating to the external sense of the allegory; for the details which he has described are of the kind (which relate) to fornicators, and likewise these words and others similar are of the kind which adulterers address to one another.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.26: [[t:0]]RECOMMENDATION CONCERNING THIS TREATISE.[[t:1]] [[t:2]]If thou desirest to understand all that (this treatise) contains, so that nothing thereof may escape thee, it is necessary to connect its chapters one with another, and in reading a chapter, one must not only aim to understand the whole of its subject, but also to grasp every word that presents itself in the course of the discourse, even though it should not form part of the (principal) subject of the chapter. For in this treatise it has never happened that I spoke as if by chance, but (everything has been said) with great exactitude and with much precision, and with care to leave no obscurity without explanation; and if there has been said (here and there) something which is not in its place, it has been only to explain some other thing in its true place. Thou must not, therefore, approach it with thy preconceived opinions, for thou wouldst do me wrong without profiting thyself; but thou must, on the contrary, first learn all that it is necessary to learn. Thou shalt make it the continual object of thy studies, for it will explain to thee the gravest obscurities of the Law, which are difficult even for every intelligent man. I adjure by God the Most High all those who shall have read the present treatise not to comment upon a single word of it and to explain nothing of it to others, save that which is already clearly explained in the words of those who have preceded me among the celebrated doctors of our Law. But (the reader) who shall have understood something of it which others of our celebrated men have not said, must not explain it to others; nor must he hasten to refute me[[fn:43]]; for it might be that what he has understood in my words was the contrary of what I intended to say, and then he would do me wrong in return for my having wished to be useful to him, and [[t:3]]he would requite good with evil[[t:4]]. On the contrary, he into whose hands (this treatise) shall fall must study it with care, and if he finds therein that which satisfies his desire[[fn:44]] (this treatise) [[t:5]]quenches his thirst[[t:6]]. Ibn-Tibbon has translated somewhat freely: [[t:7]]ואם ירפא לו מדוה לבבו[[t:8]], [[t:9]]and if it heals the sickness of his heart;[[t:10]] however, Maimonides himself had advised the translator to render these words by [[t:11]]ואם רוה צמאו[[t:12]], as is seen in the supplement of which we have just spoken in the preceding note. Instead of [[t:13]]מדוה[[t:14]], a manuscript of the Hebrew version bears [[t:15]]מחום[[t:16]], and in the margin is read the variant [[t:17]]ואם ירוה לו צמאו[[t:18]]. One may compare hereafter, Part I[[t:19]][[t:20]], at the end of chapter 45, where the words [[t:21]]מא ישפי גלילך[[t:22]] are rendered by [[t:23]]מה שירוה צמאך[[t:24]]. — Instead of [[t:25]]שפת[[t:26]] [[t:27]](شَفَتْ)[[t:28]], as we have written in our text, we read [[t:29]]שפאת[[t:30]] in all the manuscripts we have consulted (to the number of [[t:31]]eight[[t:32]]), as well as in the supplement to the letter of Maimonides of which we have just spoken.[[t:33]], were it but upon a single point of all that is obscure, he must thank God and be content with what he has understood of it. If he finds therein absolutely nothing that is useful to him, he must consider it as if it had never been composed; but if it seems to him that some harm results therefrom in relation to his opinions, he must interpret (my words) [[t:34]]in such a manner as to judge me favourably[[t:35]] ([[t:36]]ידין לכף זכות[[t:37]]), even were it by the most far-fetched interpretation, as has been prescribed to us with regard to our common people, and with all the more reason with regard to our scholars and the pillars of our Law, who strive to teach us the truth according to their faculty.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.7: S[[t:0]]EVENTH CAUSE[[t:1]]: The necessity of the discourse, when dealing with very obscure things whose details must be in part concealed and in part revealed. For sometimes one finds oneself forced, in emitting an opinion, to express oneself in such a way as to affirm a certain proposition, while in another place one finds oneself forced to express oneself in such a way as to affirm a proposition which is in contradiction with the first. The vulgar must in no way perceive the place where the contradiction exists, and the author sometimes seeks all manner of expedients to conceal it[[fn:52]], admitted by the Peripatetics, nevertheless admits it as a premise in demonstrations relating to the most important metaphysical questions, as he himself declares in ch. LXXI of Part I[[t:2]][[t:3]] and at the beginning of Part II[[t:4]][[t:5]].[[t:6]].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.15: Do you not see, moreover, that God the Most High, desiring to perfect us and to improve the state of our societies by His practical laws — [which can only be accomplished after (the establishment of) certain rational dogmas, the first condition of which is to understand the divinity according to our faculty, a thing which can only take place by means of metaphysical science, which in its turn can only follow upon physical science; for the latter is contiguous[[fn:28]]. The version of Al-Harizi bears: [[t:0]]כי המרע הטבעי הוא אחרון למדע האלהי[[t:1]]. This translator read [[t:2]]מתאבׄר[[t:3]] [[t:4]](متأخر)[[t:5]], a reading which is indeed found in the two manuscripts of the library of Leyden, but which offers no plausible sense and accords ill with the words found immediately after. The author intends to say that there is no intermediate science between physics and metaphysics, and that in the order of studies the former must precede the latter. The entire course of philosophical studies was divided, among the Arabian Peripatetics, notably since Avicenna, into three parts: 1st, logic; 2nd, physics (including therein mathematics and astronomy); 3rd, metaphysics. Compare Maimonides, in the present work, Part I[[t:6]]st[[t:7]], ch. 34 (at the 3[[t:8]]rd[[t:9]] [[t:10]]cause[[t:11]]), fol. 39 [[t:12]]a[[t:13]] of our Arabic text. See also my article [[t:14]]Ibn-Sina[[t:15]] in the [[t:16]]Dict. des sciences philos[[t:17]]., vol. III, p. 175.[[t:18]] to metaphysics and precedes it in instruction, which is clear to him who has pursued these studies] — (do you not see, I say,) that He has placed at the opening of His book the account of the creation, which is physical science, as we have explained? But because of the gravity and importance of this matter, and because our faculty is insufficient to understand the gravest of subjects in all its reality[[fn:29]], there have been chosen, to speak to us of the profound subjects with which the divine wisdom judged it necessary to entertain us, allegories, enigmas, and words extremely obscure, as (the doctors) have said: “To expound the power of the work of creation to mortals is an impossible thing; therefore Scripture has told thee in an obscure manner: [[t:19]]In the beginning God created, etc[[t:20]].” They have thus warned thee that the things mentioned are [[t:21]]obscure[[t:22]]. Thou knowest also these words of Solomon: [[t:23]]That which is, is far off[[t:24]] ([[t:25]]from our conception[[t:26]]); [[t:27]]and exceeding deep, who can find it out[[t:28]] (Ecclesiastes, 7, 25)? To speak of all these subjects, homonymous words have been employed, so that the vulgar might take them in a certain sense according to the measure of their intelligence and the weakness of their conception, and that the perfect man who has received instruction might take them in another sense.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.18: And since I have spoken of allegories, we shall state a proposition which is this: “It must be known that the key to understanding all that the prophets have said, and to knowing it in all its reality, is to understand the allegories and their meaning, and to know how to interpret their words.” Thou knowest what the Most High has said: [[t:0]]And I have used similitudes by the ministry of the prophets[[t:1]] (Hos., XII, 11); and thou knowest also this other passage: [[t:2]]Son of man, put forth a riddle, and speak a parable[[t:3]] (Ezek., 17, 2). Thou knowest also that it is because of the frequent use of allegories by the prophets that the prophet said: They say of me, [[t:4]]Doth he not speak parables?[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]Ib[[t:7]]., XXI, 5)? Thou knowest, finally, how Solomon began (his book): [[t:8]]To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings[[t:9]] (Prov., 1, 6). And in the Midrash[[fn:34]] ([[t:10]]שיל השירים רבה[[t:11]], fol. 1 [[t:12]]d[[t:13]]).[[t:14]] it is said: “To what were the words of the Torah like before Solomon appeared? To a well whose cold water was situated in the depths, so that no one could drink thereof. What then did an intelligent man do? He fastened ropes one to another and cords one to another, and then he drew and drank. Thus it was that Solomon passed[[fn:35]]. In the passage of the Midrash indicated in the preceding note, one reads more regularly: [[t:15]]כך מדבר לדבר יממשל למשל עמד שלמה על סודה של תורה[[t:16]].[[t:17]] from one allegory to another and from one discourse to another until he fathomed the words of the Torah.” Such are the textual words. I do not think that among men endowed with good sense there is a single one who imagines that the [[t:18]]words of the Torah[[t:19]] to which allusion is here made, and which one has sought to understand by the (prior) intelligence of the meaning of the allegories, are the precepts concerning the construction of tabernacles, the palm branches, and the law relating to the four guardians[[fn:36]], Part II[[t:20]]nd[[t:21]], treatise [[t:22]]Shebu’oth[[t:23]] or of [[t:24]]Oaths[[t:25]], ch. VIII); but it consists in the fundamental principles of the faith and in the profound subjects with which Theology occupies itself.[[t:26]]; on the contrary, the aim here was, without doubt, the understanding of profound things. It is said in the same place (of the Midrash): “The Rabbins say: If anyone loses a shekel or a pearl in his house, he has but to light a wick (of the value) of an obol to find the pearl; likewise the allegory in itself is nothing, but by means of the allegory thou understandest the words of the Torah.” Such again are their textual words. And observe well that they say clearly that the interior of the words of the Torah is the pearl, and that the exterior sense of every allegory is nothing, and that they compare the hidden sense represented in the exterior words of the allegory to a pearl which someone has lost in his house, which is dark and filled with furniture. This pearl exists, but he sees it not and knows not where it is: it is therefore as if it had passed out of his possession, since he has no means of profiting thereby until he lights the lamp as has been said; and it is to this that the understanding of the meaning of the allegory is likened.

root.text.Part 1..9.5: Likewise, when it concerns the arrival of a catastrophe upon a nation or a country, by reason of the eternal will of God, — wherein the prophetic books, before describing this calamity, first say that God, after having visited the actions of these people, caused punishment to descend upon them, — the expression [[t:0]]to descend[[t:1]] is also employed for this; for man is too small a thing for his actions to be visited, so that he should suffer the penalty thereof, were it not by the will (of God)[[fn:107]] to indicate that the punishment comes from the supreme divine will; for it cannot be admitted that God decrees punishment solely as a result of the evil actions of men, which would suppose that God can be influenced and change His will. On the important problem of the foreknowledge of God and the free will of man, one may see the [[t:2]]3rd[[t:3]] part of this work, chap. XVII et seq.[[t:4]].
