root.text.Part 1..1.4: Hearken now to the manner in which we replied thereto. O thou, said we, who examinest things with a superficial and unreflecting mind[[fn:70]], that is to say, according to that which first presenteth itself to the mind[[t:0]], and who imaginest thou understandest a book, a guide for the ancients and the moderns, by perusing it in some moments of leisure snatched from the pleasures of wine and cohabitation, as one would peruse some book of history or some poem! stay thy course and examine; for the matter is not such as thou didst at first believe, but such as it shall manifest itself when that which I am about to say hath been considered. The reason which God caused to emanate upon man, and which constituteth his final perfection, is that which Adam possessed before his disobedience; it is on account thereof that it was said of him that he was made [[t:1]]in the image of God and after His likeness[[t:2]], and it is because of it that speech was addressed to him and that he received commandments, as the Scripture saith: [[t:3]]And the Lord God commanded[[t:4]], etc. (Genesis, ii, 16), for commandments cannot be given to animals nor to him who possesseth not reason. By reason one distinguisheth between the [[t:5]]true[[t:6]] and the [[t:7]]false[[t:8]], and this faculty he (Adam) possessed perfectly and completely; but the [[t:9]]base[[t:10]] and the [[t:11]]beautiful[[t:12]] exist in the domain of [[t:13]]probable opinions[[t:14]], and not in [[t:15]]intelligible things[[t:16]][[fn:71]], Book I, ch. 1). The Stagirite recogniseth four species of syllogisms, of which the first two are: [[t:17]]the demonstrative[[t:18]], which hath for its basis principles of absolute truth and self-evident, being founded in the intellect, and [[t:19]]the dialectical[[t:20]], which proceedeth from [[t:21]]probable opinions[[t:22]] ([[t:23]]ἐξ ἐνδόξων[[t:24]]), and which hath for its basis the suffrages of the whole or the plurality of men, or only those of the whole or the plurality of the wise, or of the most illustrious among them. Good and evil, virtues and vices, belong to the domain of [[t:25]]probable opinions[[t:26]], and have no relation to God nor to the pure intellect (See [[t:27]]Nicomachean Ethics[[t:28]], Book VII, ch. 1). The Arabic word [[t:29]]אלמשהוראת[[t:30]], which signifieth [[t:31]]things generally known[[t:32]] or [[t:33]]celebrated things[[t:34]], here evidently designateth things admitted by opinion and correspondeth to the Greek term [[t:35]]τὰ ἔνδοξα[[t:36]]; the Hebrew versions render this word by [[t:37]]המפורסמות[[t:38]]. The Greek word [[t:39]]ἔνδοξος[[t:40]] having at once the two significations which we have just indicated, the Arabs have rendered it by a word which signifieth [[t:41]]generally known[[t:42]] or [[t:43]]celebrated[[t:44]], although this word doth not render with exactitude the idea of Aristotle. Thus, for example, these words: Δ[[t:45]]ιαλεϰτιϰὸς δέ συלλογισμὸς ὁ ἐξ ἐνδόξων συלλογιζόμενος[[t:46]] ([[t:47]]Top.[[t:48]], I, 1), "the dialectical syllogism is that which resulteth [[t:49]]from probable opinions[[t:50]]", have been thus rendered in the Arabic version: [[t:51]]والقياس الجدلى هو الذى ينتج من مقدمات ذائعة[[t:52]] . For the word [[t:53]]ذايعة[[t:54]] a marginal variant, in the Arabic MS. No. 882 A, giveth the synonym [[t:55]]مشهورة[[t:56]] , which is the term generally employed by the Arabic philosophers. Thus expresseth himself Ibn-Roschd, in his [[t:57]]Compendium of the Organon[[t:58]], at the commencement of the [[t:59]]كتاب الجدل[[t:60]] (Book of Dialectic), corresponding to the Topics of Aristotle[[t:61]]; for it is not said that this proposition: [[t:62]]the heaven is spherical[[t:63]], is beautiful, nor that this other: [[t:64]]the earth is flat[[t:65]], is base; but one is called [[t:66]]true[[t:67]] and the other [[t:68]]false.[[t:69]] Thus in our language we employ (in speaking) of the [[t:70]]true[[t:71]] and the [[t:72]]false[[t:73]] the words [[t:74]]emeth[[t:75]] ([[t:76]]אמת[[t:77]]) and [[t:78]]sheker[[t:79]] ([[t:80]]שקר[[t:81]]), and for [[t:82]]beautiful[[t:83]] and [[t:84]]base[[t:85]] we say [[t:86]]tob[[t:87]] ([[t:88]]טוב[[t:89]]) and [[t:90]]ra’[[t:91]] ([[t:92]]רע[[t:93]]). By reason, therefore, man distinguisheth the [[t:94]]true[[t:95]] from the [[t:96]]false[[t:97]], and this taketh place in all intelligible things. When, therefore, he (Adam) was yet in his most perfect and complete state, having only his primitive nature and his intelligible notions, on account of which it was said of him: [[t:98]]And Thou hast made him a little lower than the divine beings[[t:99]] (Ps. viii, 6), there was in him no faculty which applied itself to [[t:100]]probable opinions[[t:101]] in any manner whatsoever, and he did not even understand them; so that that which is most manifestly base in respect of [[t:102]]probable opinions[[t:103]], that is to say, to uncover the shameful parts, was not at all base for him, and he did not even understand the baseness thereof. But when, disobeying, he inclined toward his desires proceeding from the imaginative faculty and toward the bodily pleasures of his senses, as the Scripture saith: ... [[t:104]]That the tree was good for food and that it was a delight to the eyes[[t:105]] (Genesis, iii, 6), he was punished by the privation of that intellectual comprehension; wherefore he transgressed[[fn:72]] The words [[t:106]]פלמא עצא[[t:107]] relate to the change which was wrought in him; the second, [[t:108]]עצא[[t:109]], to the material disobedience.[[t:110]] the commandment which had been given him on account of his reason, and, having obtained the knowledge of [[t:111]]probable opinions[[t:112]], he was absorbed by that which he was to find base or beautiful, and he then knew the value of the thing which had escaped him and of which he had been despoiled, and into what state he had fallen. Therefore it was said: [[t:113]]And ye shall be as Elohim, knowing good and evil[[t:114]] ([[t:115]]Ibid.[[t:116]], iii, 5), and it was not said: knowing the [[t:117]]false[[t:118]] and the [[t:119]]true[[t:120]], or: understanding the [[t:121]]false[[t:122]] and the [[t:123]]true;[[t:124]] whereas in the domain of the [[t:125]]necessary[[t:126]][[fn:73]] in itself; the author meaneth that the pure intellect hath only to occupy itself with the true and the false. Good and evil belong to the domain of probable opinion.[[t:127]] there is no good nor evil at all, but only the false and the true. — Consider also these words: [[t:128]]And the eyes of them both were opened, and they[[t:129]] [[t:130]]KNEW[[t:131]] [[t:132]]that they were naked[[t:133]] ([[t:134]]Ibid.[[t:135]], iii, 7). It is not said: And the eyes of them both were opened, and they [[t:136]]saw;[[t:137]] for that which man had [[t:138]]seen[[t:139]] before, he [[t:140]]saw[[t:141]] also after. It was not that there was upon the eye a veil which was subsequently removed; but there came upon him another state in which he found base that which he had not found base before.
